### 12.6 The Node line — Node 26 adopted early, deliberately

Verified against `nodejs/Release` on **18 August 2026**:

| Line | Status on 18 Aug 2026 | Active LTS from | Maintenance | End of life |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v24 "Krypton" | Active LTS | 2025-10-28 | 2026-10-20 | 2028-04-30 |
| **v26** | **Current** | **2026-10-28** | 2027-10-20 | **2029-04-30** |
| v25 | End of life | never | 2026-04-01 | 2026-06-01 |

**Decision: pin 26.7.0 now.** This is a knowing, time-boxed departure from the standing rule that production runs Active or Maintenance LTS and never Current. It was taken with the alternative — 24.19 until 28 October — put and declined.

**The reasoning for it.** v26 is the destination on any timeline: it becomes Active LTS on 28 October 2026, ten weeks from this decision and well inside a build estimated at 8–12 months, and it is supported to April 2029 against v24's April 2028. v24 enters Maintenance on 20 October, so adopting 26 now means the runtime is never migrated mid-build.

**What is being accepted.** Until 28 October, 26.x carries no LTS stability commitment, and the ecosystem writes support matrices and ships native prebuilt binaries against LTS lines, so a missing prebuild or an untested combination is likelier here than on 24. v26 is an even-numbered line and *will* reach LTS, which makes this a timing bet rather than a line bet; v25 is the shape of the risk on a line that never does (end of life eight months after release, never LTS).

**Four controls, in force until 28 October 2026:**

1. **Pin the exact patch — 26.7.0 — not a floating `26`.** On a Current line a patch can carry more change than on an LTS line, so each bump is an explicit decision with a re-verification date, never an implicit pickup.
2. **Laptops, the Docker base image and CI run the same 26.7.0.** Dev parity is doing real work here (§12.5.10); on a Current runtime a version split between host and image is the most likely source of a "works locally" failure.
3. **A native-module or prebuild failure is a Node-version hypothesis first.** On an LTS line that would be an unlikely cause; for these ten weeks it is the first thing to check, before the dependency itself.
4. **Any 26.x patch bump inside the window re-runs the full gate set** before acceptance — boundary rules, RLS probes, contract tests, coverage floors, accessibility, injection corpus, cross-browser, `BILLING_ENABLED=false`.

**Scheduled action — on or after 28 October 2026:** confirm v26 has entered Active LTS, record the confirmation date against the §12.1 pin, and **retire this exception**. No migration is involved; the deviation closes by the calendar. Controls 1 and 3 relax to normal practice at that point; controls 2 and 4 are standing policy regardless.

### 12.5 Infrastructure, tooling and operational values

Decided 18 August 2026, closing §18.2's fourteen "the sources are silent" entries. Taken as one decision rather than fourteen because the parts constrain each other: the compute provider determines what "independent of the hosting provider" can mean for the archive (NFR-72), the archive provider determines the backup plan, and NFR-69's wording already narrows the secret store.

| Concern | Decision |
|---|---|
| Compute (OQ-9) | **Hetzner Cloud, Falkenstein (DE)** — VM-1, VM-2, VM-3. Off-site copy to Helsinki (FI) |
| CDN, DNS, TLS (OQ-10) | **No CDN at MVP.** DNS at Hetzner. **TLS terminates at `edge` (Caddy)** |
| Object storage (OQ-11) | **Scaleway Object Storage, Paris** — versioning + Object Lock (Compliance), Glacier for the fiscal archive. **A different provider from compute, on purpose** |
| Transactional email (OQ-12) | **Mailjet (EU)** behind `EmailPort` — one of four adapters the platform can run without a code change |
| Secrets (OQ-13) | **Self-hosted OpenBao on VM-3.** SOPS + age only for the pre-OpenBao bootstrap `.env` |
| CI (OQ-14) | **GitHub Actions.** CI holds no long-lived production credentials |
| Provisioning (OQ-15) | **Ansible** from foundation stage · **OpenTofu** when the DR runbook is written · Compose for the workload |
| Test tooling (OQ-16) | **Jest + ts-jest** in `apps/api` (both modes); **Vitest** in `apps/{web,admin}` and `packages/*`; Playwright for E2E |
| Admin token handler (OQ-17) | **A route on `api`** — not a Caddy module, not a separate service |
| Rate limits and tokens (OQ-19) | Values in §12.5.6 |
| Non-fiscal retention (OQ-20) | Schedule in §12.5.7 |
| Redis durability (OQ-21) | **RDB snapshots on a volume; AOF off; `maxmemory-policy noeviction`** |
| Backups (OQ-22) | 35-day PITR · 12 monthly · 6 yearly Object-Locked · quarterly rehearsal, one per year provider-independent |
| Chromium (OQ-27) | Derived from the Playwright pin — 1.62.1 ships **Chromium 151.0.7922.34** |

#### 12.5.1 Compute, network and the storage split

**Hetzner Cloud, Falkenstein (DE)** for all three VMs. EU-owned, so no CLOUD Act argument has to be made in a compliance product's sub-processor register; lowest per-vCPU price in the EU field, which is what makes NFR-47's €0.50 per free-tier organization comfortable at 2,000 organizations rather than tight; and plain VMs suit the Compose topology, which does not want a managed control plane. No multi-AZ within a location — already priced in, since NFR-48 is scoped to application availability precisely because `edge`, `redis` and VM-1 are unreplicated (R-11, T-7).

**No CDN at MVP.** At ~150 peak concurrent sessions and under 100 GB there is no performance case, and both ways of adding one cost something real: proxying terminates TLS at a third party that then sees every request, and full-strict passthrough adds a hop for almost nothing. Static assets are served by Next.js and Caddy with long-lived immutable cache headers. Reopens only as part of NFR-48's standing second-app-VM alternative (OQ-4).

**Object storage is Scaleway (Paris), deliberately a different provider from compute.** Object Lock in **Compliance mode** is the deciding capability, not a preference: under it an object cannot be overwritten or deleted by anyone — owner and administrator included — until retention expires, which is what DR-6's append-only guarantee and NFR-72's six-year statutory archive actually require. Verified against Scaleway's documentation on 18 Aug 2026: Object Lock requires versioning, cannot be disabled once enabled, and is supported on the Glacier class. Buckets: `esg-fiscal-archive` (locked, Glacier), `esg-exports`, `esg-backups`.

**Staging differs on both counts** (23 Oct 2026, §10.5): a shared host in Moldova rather than Hetzner, proxied by
Cloudflare, with its exports in the development stack's S3 gateway. This section describes production.

The provider split is load-bearing. NFR-72 requires fiscal documents retrievable "independently of the application, the database and the hosting provider", and `non_functional_requirements.md` OQ-14 records that NFR-36 only ever tests independence from the *application* — so the strongest clause is asserted and unverified. Putting the archive on a different provider from the VMs makes provider-independence **true by construction**, and the rehearsal in §12.5.8 makes it testable.

**Providers evaluated and rejected for storage.** AWS S3 and Google Cloud Storage — excluded on ownership, not capability: both are US-controlled, which turns NFR-27's residency assertion into a transfer-mechanism argument for a product whose whole proposition is regulatory compliance. **bunny.net** — EU-owned (Slovenia) and attractive on price and residency, but Edge Storage is positioned as CDN origin storage and **no Object Lock, versioning or WORM retention capability could be confirmed from its documentation**. For a six-year statutory archive an unconfirmed WORM capability is disqualifying on its own: the requirement is that deletion be structurally impossible, and that cannot rest on an assumption. bunny.net remains the strongest candidate to revisit for OQ-10 — CDN and DNS — if the second application VM is ever added, where its ownership and price are advantages and no WORM guarantee is needed.

#### 12.5.2 Transactional email — provider-swappable by construction

**Mailjet (EU/France)** at MVP, reached only through an `EmailPort` behind a DI token, per P-7 and D-8's adapter pattern. NFR-84 and NFR-108 need SPF/DKIM/DMARC alignment, ≥ 99% accepted delivery and — the part that eliminates most candidates — per-message bounce and complaint events fed back against the notification record (FR-157, NFR-107). Mailjet is EU-resident with a mature event webhook, so NFR-27 needs no transfer-mechanism argument.

**Switching providers must be a configuration change, not a code change**, and three rules make that true rather than aspirational:

- **No vendor type crosses the adapter boundary** (P-7). `EmailPort` speaks in platform terms — recipient, template key, locale, idempotency key, and three provider-neutral additions since: the unsubscribe's two addresses (task 52.2), the operator a footer names (task 225) and a reply-to address, the support mail's (task 77) — and returns a platform result. No Mailjet SDK type, error class or status string appears in `modules/*`, and dependency-cruiser enforces it.
- **Retry and suppression semantics live in the worker, not in provider configuration.** NFR-107's exponential schedule bounded at 24 hours and its hard-bounce suppression are ours. A provider that offers its own retry is told not to use it. This is what makes the swap LSP-clean: a different adapter cannot change caller behaviour, because the behaviour is not in the adapter.
- **Inbound events normalise at the adapter.** Every provider spells bounces, complaints and deferrals differently; the adapter maps them onto one platform event vocabulary before anything else sees them, so FR-157's records and NFR-109's retention are provider-independent.

The adapter pattern is the one the payment rails and `EInvoicingPort` already use (D-7, D-8). Second candidate on file: **Scaleway TEM**, which consolidates to two providers and is the swap if the Mailjet relationship fails. **Postmark** has the best transactional deliverability in the field and is US-resident. GDPR would permit it under the EU–US Data Privacy Framework, but **NFR-27 relies on no adequacy decision and no SCCs** (amended 25 Aug 2026, `non_functional_requirements.md` OQ-16), so Postmark is excluded by the platform's own rule and not by law: an adequacy decision can fall, and a rule that rests on one has to be re-argued each time.

**The transport is SMTP and the provider is an environment value** (`task.md` 51.1). Every candidate above exposes SMTP, so a swap is a configuration change, not a new adapter class. What is *not* provider-neutral is the inbound leg: bounce and complaint webhooks differ per provider and normalise at the adapter, which is where a swap actually costs work (`task.md` 51.4).

#### 12.5.3 Secrets — the open question was already half-decided

**Self-hosted OpenBao on VM-3.** NFR-69 requires secrets held "in a managed secret manager, scoped per environment and **access-logged**", and SOPS-encrypted files in a repository cannot produce an access log: decryption happens on whatever host holds the age key, unobserved. SOPS alone would have needed an NFR amendment. Self-hosting rather than buying follows the argument already made for observability — it keeps NFR-27 trivially true and adds no sub-processor — and for a platform holding payment-rail credentials and fiscal transmission keys, a real audit log of secret access is proportionate.

SOPS + age is retained for exactly one purpose: encrypting the bootstrap `.env` that Compose needs before OpenBao is reachable. Unseal keys are split and held out-of-band, and the seal/unseal procedure is a runbook deliverable.

**Staging holds its secrets in a root-readable `.env` on its host** (23 Oct 2026, §10.5) — synthetic values protecting
synthetic data. OpenBao and NFR-69's access log are production's.

#### 12.5.4 CI, and what it may not hold

**GitHub Actions** on hosted `ubuntu-latest` runners. The gates — boundary rules, RLS probes, contract tests, coverage floors, accessibility, injection corpus, cross-browser, `BILLING_ENABLED=false` — all run on a stock Linux runner: PostgreSQL 18 and Redis, Chromium via Playwright, veraPDF for NFR-82, headless LibreOffice Calc for NFR-20's CI half.

**The database comes from the Compose stack, not from `services:` containers (20 Aug 2026, task 17).** `infra/postgres/init/init.sh` creates the four roles of §7.6 and a `services:` block has no clean way to run it, so CI would carry a second copy of the role split, and the copy CI ran would be the one no developer ever executes. `pnpm dev:up` gives the roles, the health checks and the init script, and `--wait` blocks until every health check passes, so no step races a half-built cluster. The suites then run against the test stack they bring up beside it (`pnpm test:stack`, §12.5.10).

**Workflow entrypoints live in `.github/workflows/`**, which is the only place GitHub reads them; §10.7's `infra/ci` holds the composite setup action every job shares (Node, pnpm, frozen install).

**Amended 24 Oct 2026 (project owner, task 224): a push confined to the two leaf applications skips the api's stack suites.** No workspace depends on `apps/web` or `apps/admin` — they are the dependency graph's leaves — so a change confined to them cannot move the outcome of a suite that exercises only the api (`pnpm e2e` is 5.3 of the stack job's 19.9 minutes). `tools/ci-scope.sh` decides, never the workflow, and anyone can run it to see what CI will skip:

- **What counts as confined.** Every path that differs is under `apps/web/` or `e2e/web/` (the tenant application), under `apps/admin/` or `e2e/admin/` (the console), or **neutral** — `docs/`, `design/`, `.gitignore` and markdown, which the workflow's push trigger already treats as unable to break a gate. Markdown under `packages/` or `config/` is not neutral: a spec reads `packages/ui`'s contrast record, and the seed's README sits in the folder the seed reader lists and ships in the api image. Any other path — a package, the lockfile, root configuration, `tools/`, `infra/`, `config/`, the browser suite's own configuration under `e2e/` — runs the whole set.
- **Against what.** The tree of the branch's last *green* push run, not the previous push: a newer push cancels an older run, and a red run followed by a confined fix would otherwise skip the very suite that went red. Trees are compared rather than history, so a force push is handled too, and with rename detection off, so a file moved out of a package counts as a change to that package. No green run to compare with, a pull request or a manual run: the whole set.
- **What a confined push skips.** In the stack job, `migrations:check`, the seed run twice, `pnpm e2e` and `pnpm e2e:worker`; in the `BILLING_ENABLED=false` job, `pnpm e2e`. The browser suite runs only its `admin` project when the console alone changed; a change to the tenant application runs all three, because three console journeys open the tenant application and the console's specs import `e2e/web/support`. The gates that need no database run whole, and so does the billing-off job's `pnpm test`, since `apps/web` reads `BILLING_ENABLED` at runtime and neither shortens the run. The images job is unchanged.
- **What it changes about a task's close.** The 6 Oct 2026 rule closes a task on the gates its change reaches because CI then runs the whole set on the push. For a confined push CI now runs no more than the close did — sound only because nothing depends on the leaves, which is why the scope stops at them and never reaches `packages/*`. A Stage still ends on `pnpm gates:clean`.
- **What would make it wrong.** A workspace that comes to depend on `apps/web` or `apps/admin`, or a skipped suite that comes to read a path counted as confined or neutral. Either makes the script's lists wrong, and the script is what changes.

**Amended 20 Nov 2026 (project owner, task 253): a run whose files a green push run already proved runs no gate.** A release merges `dev` into `main` through a pull request, and both the pull request's test merge and the merge commit on `main` hold `dev`'s tree byte for byte — so each release ran the whole set three times over one tree, the last two proving nothing the first had not. `tools/ci-scope.sh` decides this too, before the confined rule, and answers `proven`:

- **What counts as proven.** The commit's tree is identical to the tree of a commit it merges in — a parent past the first, which for a pull request's test merge is the head it would merge — and that commit has a green **push** run of the Gates workflow. Identity, not a diff: one changed byte anywhere runs the rules above. A push run is required because it is what publishes images under its sha; a feature branch's pull request never qualifies, its head having no push run.
- **For a pull request too**, where the confined rule never applies: the owner chose both on 20 Nov 2026, so a release costs one full run, `dev`'s push.
- **Never on a re-run or a manual run.** A second attempt at any run, or a run asked for by hand, takes the whole set — someone asking again is asking for all of it.
- **What a proven run does.** The three gate jobs and the images job skip. On a push, a `promote` job copies the four images published under the proving commit's sha to this commit's, in the registry and as carbon copies (`docker buildx imagetools create --prefer-index=false`, the same manifest digests) — so what a deploy of this sha pulls is byte for byte what the gates passed, which a rebuild could only approximate. The run's summary names the proving commit and its run.
- **What it costs.** Every job waits on one `scope` job, which replaced task 224's per-job scope step: a job can be skipped only by reading an answer from a job before it. A gate job reads `!= 'proven'` under `!cancelled()`, so a scope job that failed runs every gate.
- **What would make it wrong.** A gate whose outcome depends on more than the tree — the runner image, a base image or an action tag that moved since the proving run — which a proven run does not re-check. Accepted: the images that ship are the ones tested, and the next full run on `dev` re-checks the environment.

**CI holds no long-lived production credentials.** Deploys use short-lived OIDC-issued credentials; CI never reads from OpenBao. A CI compromise must not be a production compromise. **Forgejo Actions** self-hosted on VM-3 is the drop-in alternative — near-identical workflow syntax — if the repository ever cannot live on GitHub.

#### 12.5.5 Provisioning, staged

Two tools with different jobs, adopted at different times.

- **Ansible** — configuration management. Describes the *state of a host*: users, SSH policy, Docker Engine, PgBouncer, pgBackRest, the node exporter, kernel parameters. It connects over SSH, needs no agent, and is idempotent, so re-running it converges a drifted host rather than duplicating work. **Adopted from foundation stage**, because host configuration drifts continuously and undocumented drift is what makes a rebuild unrepeatable.
- **OpenTofu** — infrastructure provisioning. Describes the *existence of resources*: the three VMs, firewall rules, DNS records, the Scaleway buckets and their lock configuration. It keeps a state file and computes the difference between declared and actual. It is the open-source fork of Terraform, under MPL rather than Terraform's BUSL licence, with an equivalent provider ecosystem for Hetzner and Scaleway. **Adopted when the DR runbook is written**, which is where it pays for itself: recovery becomes an apply against a second region instead of a memory of what was clicked.

The staging is deliberate: adopting both at once front-loads two unfamiliar tools onto the foundation sprint, and Ansible pays immediately while OpenTofu pays at the first disaster-recovery rehearsal. The workload itself stays Docker Compose; the directories are `infra/ansible` and, later, `infra/tofu`.

**Neither reaches staging** (23 Oct 2026, §10.5): its host is shared and administered for every tenant on it, so this
platform sets up what it needs there once — the vhost, the certificate, a pinned deploy key, a checkout — and deploys
through `infra/staging/deploy.sh`. Ansible and OpenTofu describe the production VMs.

**Both are deploy-path tooling and neither is a developer-workstation prerequisite.** "Adopted from foundation stage" is when the tool enters the project, not when it is installed on a laptop. They run in one of two places and nowhere else:

| | Where it runs | Installed as |
|---|---|---|
| Normal operation | The CI runner (§12.5.4) | A pinned job step, not a machine-level install |
| Initial bootstrap and disaster recovery | One operator machine | A deliberate, documented install — the estate has to exist before CI can deploy to it |

The bootstrap case is the only reason a person installs either locally: CI deploys to infrastructure, and infrastructure is what OpenTofu creates. A developer building `apps/*` or `packages/*` never needs either tool.

#### 12.5.6 Test tooling, coverage floors, rate limits and token bounds

**Jest + ts-jest** in `apps/api`, which covers HTTP and worker modes alike — there is no separate `apps/worker` package, only a second entrypoint in the same image (§5.4, §10.7). Jest is NestJS's default, and AD-13 already assumes ts-jest in its argument for pinning TypeScript at 6.x. **Vitest** in `apps/web`, `apps/admin` and `packages/*` — `apps/admin` is Vite, where Vitest is native and materially faster on component suites. One documented exception costs less than forcing either runner across both sides. **Playwright** for E2E and cross-browser, already pinned.

**Coverage floors** — NFR-88 names five components and requires reporting per component, never as a project average. That per-component reporting is the requirement's real content; these are its missing values, closing `non_functional_requirements.md` OQ-10.

| Component | Line | Branch | Measured over | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Invoice numbering | 100% | **100%** | not built — task 57 | DR-8 gapless numbering per series per year. A missed branch is a fiscal compliance defect, and the unit is small and pure, so 100% is cheap |
| VAT calculation | 100% | **100%** | not built — task 61 | Same argument. Wrong VAT on an immutable, transmitted fiscal document cannot be corrected in place |
| Emissions calculator | 95% | 90% | `apps/api/src/modules/core/calculator/domain/` | Feeds B3 and a published report; factor-set version pinning (DR-4) multiplies the branch count |
| Validation engine | 95% | 90% | `packages/validation/src/rules/` | Coverage is over the config interpreter (AD-4), with the rule corpus as fixtures |
| Entitlement service | 90% | 85% | not built — task 54 | `allow / deny / allow_with_warning` across every gated action; must hold with `BILLING_ENABLED=false` |

Project-wide floor 80%, reported alongside but never in place of the five.

**Measured since task 205, and this table is what the gate reads** (8 Oct 2026). `pnpm test:coverage` runs every
unit suite with coverage on and then `tools/check-coverage.mjs`, which takes each floor and its path from the rows
above — so a floor is moved here and nowhere else. A row *not built* names the task that builds its component and
fills in its path at that task's close; the gate refuses such a row once its task has left `docs/task.md`. **The
project-wide figure is reported and not yet enforced**: it stood at 71.76% of lines when the gate was built, and
§12.5.6's task-205 row records that deferral with the rest of the gate's decisions.

**Rate limits, lockout and token bounds** — closing OQ-19 and `non_functional_requirements.md` OQ-4, whose qualitative terms left NFR-64 and FR-4's "threshold" with no pass condition.

| Control | Value |

| Social sign-in — task 24 | 5 attempts / 15 min per (IP, provider): the account is unknowable before the exchange the throttle guards, so the key is stricter than the per-(IP, account) intent above |
| Invitation issue and resend — task 141 | 5 emails / 15 min per (organization, address), one key shared by both routes and carrying no IP: what is rationed is mail to one mailbox from one organization, 20 an hour |
| Account lockout — FR-4's "threshold" | 10 consecutive failures; released by reset link or by a Platform Administrator on A-02, stating a reason (FR-209; 5 Oct 2026, 182/1) |
| Unauthenticated API, per IP | 60 req / min at `edge` |
| Provider webhooks (`/api/v1/webhooks/*`), per source IP | **600 req / min at `edge`**, a bucket separate from the unauthenticated budget; 429 beyond it, recovered by provider retry (AD-6 dedup). Alert at 70% sustained. **Set 18 Aug 2026** |
| Published content read (`/api/v1/content/*`) — task 76 | **Generic unauthenticated traffic**: the 60 req / min per-IP budget above, at `edge`; not an auth path's 5 in 15 minutes, which would refuse a reader opening four articles, and not the webhook bucket (182/45). Enforced by the edge (task 71.1), which honours this row; the api enforces nothing of its own, since `req.ip` is the proxy's address until task 71 sets `trust proxy` (the task-76 row (6)). **Set 5 Oct 2026, named 30 Oct 2026** |

The edge's unauthenticated budget applies on top once 71.1 lands (the task-77 row (6)). **Set 30 Oct 2026** |

Since task 50.1.4 the link carrying a token is also kept sealed on its notice as evidence (OQ-54's second copy). **The unsubscribe token is outside this row** — an HMAC-SHA256 over its subject, compared in constant time, neither random nor stored nor single-use (the task-52.2 row (4)) |

The two are equal in the second policy on purpose — declining *keep me signed in* must not yield a session that rolls indefinitely through use, so there the absolute cap always binds |

Cost, once, on deploy: a challenge sealed by the previous build lacks the field and reads as no challenge, so anyone mid-factor retypes their password — a five-minute window. **Set 4 Sep 2026** |
| Password policy — nowhere stated before OQ-51 | ≥ 8 and ≤ 128 characters, requiring a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter, a digit and one further character. **Set 20 Aug 2026** |

Enforced at the point of use from task 19; the reclaiming sweep — a scheduled job deleting by the same predicate — is task 200's, the worker's nightly job since 21 Nov 2026 (OQ-52; §12.5.6's task-200 row). **Set 20 Aug 2026** **Amended 14 Sep 2026** (project owner, task 155): an account registered through a provider that has not completed its setup (`awaiting_setup`) is deleted on the same rule, seven days after registration; an account moved into setup from `active` is not, since it may hold organizations (§12.5.6's task-155 row). |

That is the opposite of the wire's default, deliberately — an absent field from a *client* means it may never have known the question, whereas an absent field in a payload **this tier sealed** dates it. **A sealed payload with no account `status`, or one this tier does not recognise, reads as `active`** (14 Sep 2026, task 155), by the same dating argument: only an active account could hold a session before that task. Known misread, **accepted because no deployment holds accounts yet** (tasks 71–72): an account that task 155's migration moves into setup while signed in passes the proxy and is refused `account-setup-required` by the api until the next rotation (at most fifteen minutes) instead of being sent to S-36; a deployment that moves signed-in accounts into setup needs the web tier to answer that refusal with S-36 first, which binds at tasks 71–72. **A cookie the session gate refuses is deleted on the redirect it answers with** (10 Sep 2026, task 112): unsealable, or past the refresh bound, it is worthless, and a declined session's cookie carries no `Max-Age`, so nothing else would remove it before the browser closes. |
| CSRF stance — OQ-33 | `SameSite=Lax` plus a same-origin proof on every state-changing request through the web pass-through (`Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin`, falling back to an Origin/Host comparison where the header is absent); Server Actions ride Next's built-in Origin/Host check. No CSRF-token machinery. **Set 21 Aug 2026** |
| Admin session cookie — task 23 | One httpOnly cookie (`easyesg_admin_session`), set by the **api itself** (OQ-17): the same AD-12 pair — ≤15-min HS256 JWT + rotating single-use refresh token — plus the operator identity block, sealed AES-256-GCM. Keys derived (HKDF, distinct labels) from one `AUTH_ADMIN_SECRET`, disjoint from the tenant realm's secrets (NFR-65). `Secure; SameSite=Strict; Path=/`, host-only on the api origin. **Set 21 Aug 2026, project owner** |
| Admin realm CORS and CSRF — task 23 | The api allows exactly the configured `ADMIN_ORIGIN`, with credentials; state-changing admin-realm requests must present an `Origin` equal to it (`Sec-Fetch-Site` alone cannot tell one sibling subdomain from another, and NFR-65 treats each as its own trust zone). `Strict` rather than the web tier's `Lax` because nothing legitimate ever arrives at the api origin by top-level navigation carrying an admin session. **Set 21 Aug 2026** |
| Admin MFA — task 23 | TOTP (RFC 6238, 30 s step, ±1 window), challenged on **every** sign-in (FR-75: without exception). The secret is provisioned with the account — UC-68's own precondition — by CLI until UC-87's screens exist (task 67); enrolment UX and recovery codes are task 27's. The secret is AES-256-GCM at rest since task 27.1, 26 Aug 2026 — see the secrets-at-rest row below. **Set 21 Aug 2026** |
| Admin factor challenge — task 23 review | **Five minutes**, stateless: A-01's two-step handshake (chosen by the project owner, 24 Aug 2026, over presentational staging) verifies the credential first and seals `{account, issuedAt}` into its own httpOnly `SameSite=Strict` cookie — no table, TTL evaluated at the point of use. Deliberately NOT single-use: a mistyped code stays on the factor step (A-01's recoverable "failed factor"), with guessing bounded exactly as the one-shot flow bounded it — both steps spend the same 5/15-min window, and factor failures count toward the ten-failure lockout. **Set 24 Aug 2026** |
| Social sign-in flow — task 24 | The OAuth redirect endpoints live on **`apps/web`** — `/auth/social/{provider}/start` and `/auth/social/{provider}/callback`, fixed and unlocalized, because they are the URIs registered at the provider. The api is the confidential client's **back channel**: `POST /auth/social/{provider}/challenge` builds the authorization URL (`state`, `nonce`, PKCE — generated api-side, behind `IdentityProviderPort`), and `POST /auth/social/{provider}/session` performs the token exchange and ID-token validation and answers with the **same session shape as password sign-in**, which web seals into the OQ-33 cookie exactly as task 22 does. The in-flight OIDC transaction (state, nonce, verifier, intent, return path) travels as web's own short-lived sealed httpOnly cookie and never reaches the browser readable. Declined: passport middleware owning api-side redirect routes — only web holds `SESSION_SECRET` and only its Route Handlers may write the session cookie, so an api-owned callback would need a one-time handoff ticket, a second credential exchange OQ-33 never reviewed. UC-05's alternate flow is carried by an **intent** on the transaction: a sign-in-intent completion that matches no linked identity and no account **offers registration rather than silently creating an account**, and a register-intent completion against an already-registered address refuses without creating a duplicate (BR-ID-3), directing the user to password sign-in; the linking route is FR-8, task 27. **Set 24 Aug 2026, project owner** **Amended 25 Sep 2026 (task 171): the callback's `iss` travels with the code.** A provider whose metadata declares `authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported` — Google's does — returns `iss` on its callback (RFC 9207), and the certified client refuses an authorization response that omits it or names another issuer. The callback forwards `iss` as the completion's optional `issuer`, the api puts it back on the reconstructed callback, and the stub provider declares and sends it as Google does. |
| Social provider configuration — task 24 | Split by sensitivity, resolving FR-82 against NFR-69 while OpenBao does not yet exist (§12.5.3). **Behaviour is config-store data** — kind `identity-provider`, scope per provider: enabled state, client id, issuer, scopes, redirect-URI allowlist — so withdrawing a provider needs no redeploy (the FR-82 clause that guards against an outage) and A-18 has data to edit. **The client secret stays an environment variable** (`AUTH_SOCIAL_<PROVIDER>_CLIENT_SECRET`, HTTP tier only, beside `AUTH_JWT_SECRET` and the pepper): a live secret in `config.entry_version` would be plaintext readable by `esg_admin_ro`, replicas and backups, against NFR-69's posture. **Recorded deferral:** FR-82's rotate-without-redeploy clause is rotation-by-restart until OpenBao exists. **Set 24 Aug 2026, project owner** **Amended 14 Sep 2026** (project owner, task 67.11): **task 154** owns OpenBao and this clause; A-18 edits the behaviour half and states where the secret is (the task-67.11 row below). |
| Invitation resend — task 26.1 | **A resend rotates the token and restarts the seven days**, on the same invitation row. FR-57's "a resend delivers the same invitation" is satisfied by the record, not the string: the row keeps its id, role and history, so S-16 shows one line per invited person. The reissued token invalidates the outstanding link immediately and leaves **exactly one live link per invitation, ever** — OQ-55's verification precedent applied to the third token kind. Declined: re-delivering the existing link unchanged, which makes an expired invitation unfixable except by revoke-and-reinvite; and re-delivering it with the expiry extended, which makes a link's lifetime unbounded. **Cost accepted:** an invitee who opens the first email after a resend gets a dead link and must use the newer one. **Set 25 Aug 2026, project owner** |
| Invitation email language — task 26.1 | **The invited address's account locale where one exists, the inviting administrator's negotiated locale otherwise** — the account's **email** language since task 52.3, chosen apart from its interface's (§12.5.6's task-52.3 row (3)) — resolved once at issue and stored on the invitation row (`identity.invitation.locale`), from where it travels in the outbox payload as the verification and reset events carry theirs. FR-169 resolves language per recipient and a worker has no `Accept-Language` to negotiate; for an invitee with no account the inviter's locale is the only evidence in the request. The lookup is server-side and its result never reaches the administrator. Declined: always using the inviter's locale, which contradicts FR-169 in terms; and resolving on the worker at send time, which carries no fallback locale there and breaks the payload shape both existing email events share. **Set 25 Aug 2026, project owner** |
| Invitation collisions — task 26.1 | **Both refused with `409`, each naming its resolving action** (NFR-79): an address held by an **active member** answers "they already have access"; one holding a **pending invitation** answers "an invitation is outstanding — resend it or revoke it". Enforced by a partial unique index on `(organization_id, lower(invited_email)) WHERE status = 'pending'` rather than by a prior read, because two simultaneous invitations of one address both pass a read-then-write check. **An expired-but-unrevoked invitation is included in that refusal**, deliberately: a partial index cannot reference `now()`, and a resend, which rotates the token and restarts the window, is what a lapsed invitation needs (UC-61 gives the administrator resend and revoke). Declined: treating a duplicate invite as a silent resend, which leaves the administrator unable to tell whether they invited or nudged and makes a re-invite at a different role a silent change or no-op; and allowing several live invitations per address, which duplicates rows on S-16 and makes FR-57's "invalidates the outstanding link" ambiguous. **Set 25 Aug 2026, project owner** |

The address is the mailbox being protected; a per-invitation key would compose with issue, because every issue mints a fresh resend budget, and exceed the ceiling. The organization qualifies the key so one tenant cannot exhaust another tenant's budget for the same person. **A success spends the window — like sign-in, unlike acceptance** (project owner, 13 Sep 2026): acceptance inverts it because a success there proves the caller held a live token, whereas here the email **is** the harm, so the admitted call is what counts. An issue refused for a collision rolls its attempt row back with the request and costs no budget, because no mail left. **`clientIp` is absent** where every other key carries one: the caller is a named Organization Administrator and their network is not what is rationed — this is a ceiling on an accountable actor, not a spam control. Task 71 must not treat these two routes as generic authenticated traffic, for the reason OQ-53 records about `register` |

It states in SQL what is true: *the bearer of this token may read this one row*, signed in or not. UC-15's acceptor reads the invitation **before** they are a member, so `app.current_org` is unbound and 26.1's tenant policy answers zero rows; S-03 also has to render the inviting organization's name to a visitor still signed out, which no policy over `app.current_user` can serve. Declined: a policy on the acceptor's own email address (`SELECT lower(email) FROM identity.account WHERE id = app.current_user`), which leaves S-03's signed-out preview unserved; dropping the preview, which contradicts S-03's stated content; and `SECURITY DEFINER`, because `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` subjects the owner to its own policies, so a definer function reading this table returns nothing (25.3). **Set 25 Aug 2026, project owner** |

Sign-in refuses an unverified account (OQ-57's `403 email-unverified`), so without this a password invitee could never reach the accept route without a second email and six steps. It is scoped by **the proxy's own list** (`apps/web/src/lib/route-access.ts`), not a second one, so the closed-by-default session gate and this branch cannot disagree about which routes those are; a route needing no session needs no organization, and `/invitation/{token}` is the case — it must be the one deep link a person who belongs nowhere is returned to. The type makes a base32 TOTP secret **unrepresentable**, binding the api, the provisioning CLI and an operator at a `psql` prompt alike (P-4); the populations are separated by alphabet — base32 draws from `A-Z2-7=`, and the envelope's lowercase `v` and `.` are outside it. Encryption is a **persistence** concern: the store adapter seals on write and opens on read, as OQ-50 puts the epoch-ms conversion there, so no use case, domain type or DTO knows the column is encrypted. An opening failure **throws**, unlike the session cookie's `null`: a secret that will not open is a wrong key or a corrupt row, and degrading it to "wrong code" would present a misconfiguration as the operator's typing. Applies to `identity.admin_account.totp_secret`, task 27.2's tenant secrets and, since task 50.1.4, `notification.notification.sealed_link`, the link a token-carrying notice sent. **Set 26 Aug 2026, project owner** |

| Secret-column classification — task 27.1 | **"A plaintext secret is unrepresentable" is a gate, not a review note.** `test/schema-invariants.e2e-spec.ts` classifies every column of the five domain schemas that holds a secret: an **encrypted** one must be of the `identity.encrypted_secret` domain, and anything else must be named as plaintext-by-design with its reason (a one-way hash is not a secret at rest, and encrypting it would add a key whose loss destroys every password in the system). A column named `%secret%` or `%password%` in neither list fails the gate. The patterns stop there deliberately: `token` and `_key` would sweep in `idempotency_key`, `attempt_key` and every `token_hash`, and a noisy rule gets switched off rather than satisfied. Task 27.2 thereby inherits the decision by construction; the shape is §7.10's audited/not-audited classification. **Set 26 Aug 2026, project owner** |

The secret is `identity.encrypted_secret` from **task 27.1**, so the tenant table has encryption at rest from the start. **Enrolment is two steps and activation needs the second**: a secret is issued, and the factor becomes active only when a current code proves the authenticator captured it, since activating on issue alone locks out anyone whose scan silently failed. **Enrolling and disenrolling both require the current password** — FR-8's rule for linking a provider, for the same reason: a second factor survives a compromised session, so a compromised session must be unable to install or strip one. Since task 155 (14 Sep 2026) no active account lacks a password, so there is no password-less case. **Set 26 Aug 2026, project owner** |
| Recovery codes — task 27.2 | **Ten codes, sixteen Crockford base32 characters each (~80 bits), SHA-256, single-use, shown exactly once.** The token row above specifies ≥ 256 bits for emailed links, a different object: a recovery code is transcribed by a person, so entropy is bounded by what a human will copy. Eighty bits keeps an **offline** attack on a stolen database dump pointless, where the fifty bits of a ten-character code would not; online guessing is bounded by the auth-path throttle and FR-4's lockout either way. **SHA-256 rather than Argon2id**, as for this section's tokens: the input is high-entropy, so a slow hash buys nothing against a dump, and since codes are indistinguishable until matched and verification tries each in turn, Argon2id would turn a sign-in step into a denial-of-service lever. Crockford's alphabet because the reader retypes from paper and `0`/`O` and `1`/`I` are where that goes wrong. **Re-issuing replaces the whole set**, and exhausting the set is a designed state the user is warned about before it arrives (UC-195). **Set 26 Aug 2026, project owner** |

So step one answers a **sealed opaque challenge in the response body** — `{ accountId, issuedAt, kind }` under AES-256-GCM, keyed by HKDF from `AUTH_JWT_SECRET` under a distinct label (`JwtAdminTokens`' one-secret-two-keys split applied to the tenant realm, no new environment variable). `apps/web` holds it in its own short-lived httpOnly cookie, as it holds task 24's OAuth transaction. Otherwise §12.5.6's admin factor row applies unchanged: **no table**, TTL evaluated at the point of use, and **deliberately not single-use**, so a mistyped code stays on the step. A challenge is not a session: it carries no token, and presenting it without a valid code yields nothing. **Set 26 Aug 2026, project owner.** **Amended 27 Aug 2026 after review:** the completion **checks FR-4's lock** (`locked_at`) before the code is verified — `SignIn`'s ordering and reason — raising `AccountLockedError`, as well as incrementing `failed_attempts`. The counter enters this step at **zero**, because the password success that produces a challenge clears it, and the window admits five attempts against a five-minute challenge, so ten consecutive failures is not a state this step can reach alone: the throttle, not the lockout, bounds guessing here. |

A `challenge` → `session` split as in UC-68 would impose a second round trip on every user to serve an opt-in minority. **The challenged answer is a 200 rather than a problem document**: nothing failed, and NFR-79's three-part refusal shape has nothing to say about a step proceeding normally. It discloses that the account has a factor only to someone who has presented the correct password, the one point at which that is knowable; NFR-64's uniform-response clause concerns the credential step before it. **Set 26 Aug 2026, project owner** |

Such a route is a password *oracle* for someone holding only a stolen session: the edge's authenticated budget is 300 req/min per organization, so an unbounded route yields eighteen thousand guesses an hour against a value people reuse across services. Naming the path rather than letting it inherit is the precedent OQ-53 and OQ-55 set. **Its own key, not sign-in's**, for `adminSignInThrottleKey`'s reason — a user fumbling their password on a settings screen has not been probing the sign-in page, and neither budget should exhaust the other. **Deliberately NOT wired to FR-4's lockout**, unlike sign-in and the factor step: the caller has proved possession of a session, and a mistyped password on a settings screen must not sign them out of every device. Reusing the reset value would make the trail state something untrue about an account the user still holds, which is the one thing an audit column must not do. FR-7's termination is **opt-in**, since the requirement says *where the user elects it*, and it spares the **current** session by construction: revoking it would sign the user out of the device they just changed their password on, which is not what "other active sessions" means. **Set 27 Aug 2026, project owner** |

Its own key, for `adminSignInThrottleKey`'s reason: someone mistyping the code their authenticator shows has not been probing passwords, and neither budget should exhaust the other. Like the re-authentication window and unlike sign-in's, it does **not** feed FR-4's lockout — the caller holds a session, and a fumbled enrolment must not sign them out everywhere. **Set 27 Aug 2026** |

| Admin sign-in in the system audit log — task 28.4 | **Every admin sign-in attempt is a row in `audit.system_audit_log`**, and A-01's LOGGED disclosure ships with it. Both outcomes are recorded — a completed sign-in and each way one fails (wrong credential, wrong factor, locked, throttled) — because a log of successes alone answers *who got in* and not *who tried*. **The row gains a pseudonymous `subject`, and the shape is the decision** (project owner, 27 Aug 2026). The table carried `actor_id` and no free-text column, so an attempt against an address matching no account was unattributable. `subject` is the **SHA-256 of the normalised presented address**, never the address: it makes "all attempts against this address" one query while the append-only, 24-month table (§12.5.7) never holds personal data it could not later remove. | A member's last activity — FR-56 | **Set 28 Sep 2026, project owner**, from a defect on S-16: *Last activity* read *not signed in yet* of every member, because `identity.membership.last_active_at`, created by task 25.1 for "task 28's guard" to write, was never written. **The rule: `AuthGuard` records the member's activity in the organization a request acts for, at a five-minute grain** — once it has resolved the active membership and passed every refusal, it asks `MEMBER_ACTIVITY_STORE` to write the request's instant unless what is recorded is within five minutes of it (`session/domain/member-activity.ts`). **Its own short transaction**, binding the organization and the member's account, never the request's: a row lock held for the request's life would make a member's parallel requests wait on each other. **Any signed-in request in that organization counts**, the unread count's minute poll included, so the column reads as *last had the app open there* — accepted by the owner over distinguishing a person's actions from a tab's polls. A request acting for no organization, and a refused one, records nothing. Declined: a write on every request (exact, but the system's busiest writer, with a member's parallel requests contending for one row); and sign-in and refresh only (cheapest, but accurate to about fifteen minutes and blind to which organization was used). | The global tier's two halves — task 30.1 | **The switch is split from the tier and appended as task 83, and the tier ships without it** (project owner, 29 Aug 2026). Task 83 has since closed: the switch is built as `PUT /api/v1/session/organization`, chosen over `POST /memberships/{id}/activation` (which names the membership when what changes is the session) and `PATCH /session` (a body that grows where today there is one mutable property) — see the row `The organization switch — task 83` in this section. Until the switch, the organization was drawn as a plate with no caret, because a control that cannot act is worse than an absent one. **UX-2 needed a second decision.** `GET /organization` is `@RequiresRole(ORGANIZATION_ADMINISTRATOR)`, so a viewer or editor could not learn which organization the request resolved to, while UX-2 binds every authenticated screen for every actor. `GET /memberships` therefore answers **`active`** on each row — `AuthGuard`'s `selectActiveMembership` result, already on the request context. That **reverses task 25.3's "No `isActive` flag"** while keeping its principle: only the server resolves the active organization, once, per request, from the session. | The e2e ceiling moves to 30 s, and the cause is the host's memory — task 85 | **`testTimeout: 30000` in `apps/api/test/jest-e2e.json`, six times jest's default** (1 Sep 2026). A page fault lands on one operation and misses its neighbours, so degradation is **episodic** rather than uniform, and it clusters in `gates` and `gates:clean`, which build immediately before `pnpm e2e`. **Two CPU hypotheses are refuted and must not be re-run**: event-loop delay and Argon2id timings did not move under CPU load. **The ceiling is not the instrument for noticing a genuine slowdown**; the per-test distribution in `apps/api/test/README.md` is, read at p50/p90, which contention barely moves. The row above explains the mechanism; this is the same fault in the `units` gate. | The permission matrix separates *inconclusive* from *admitted* — task 88 | **Three problem types are evidence of nothing and must never read as admission: `internal`, `rate-limited`, `session-expired`** (1 Sep 2026), plus any `5xx` carrying no problem+json at all. A **500** means the guard chain's verdict is *unknown*, a **429** means the request was refused before the guards could decide, and a **`session-expired`** is `AuthGuard` refusing with a type `route-matrix.e2e-spec.ts` does not list; read as `admitted`, a token lapsing mid-run would turn every remaining route into a silent admission. **A status alone cannot make this call**: `POST /auth/session` is `@Public()` and answers `401 credential-invalid` to the matrix's empty body, which *is* admission. The discriminator is the problem **type**; the status is only the backstop for a crash that never reached the filter. The classification is a pure function with its four arms under test, because the arm that matters almost never fires against a live server | task 28.2, task 88, NFR-90 |
| An e2e request reaches the server it was addressed to — the harness binds `127.0.0.1` | **Set 14 Sep 2026, project owner, from an investigation of three failures recorded as unreproduced** (tasks 67.4, 144). **The cause is a port displacement** — not the application, and not the host's memory. supertest's `serverAddress` calls `app.listen(0)` with **no host** for every request against an unlistened server, which binds the IPv6 wildcard, and then requests `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`; on macOS a wildcard binding does not stop another process binding the same port on `127.0.0.1`, which the kernel then prefers, so that process answers our request. **The fix is a test-process patch, `apps/api/test/support/supertest-loopback.ts`**: supertest's per-request server listens on `127.0.0.1`, and the request is sent once it is listening, so the address bound and the address requested are one. **It patches supertest rather than `http.Server#listen`**, because a `listen` naming a host binds asynchronously while supertest reads `address()` synchronously on the next line. **Central rather than per suite** (owner's decision): each of ~40 suites listening explicitly would work until the next one omitted it — `close-connections.ts`'s reason (tasks 85, 87) for patching the test process. `supertest-loopback.e2e-spec.ts` proves it and fails with the patch removed; it reaches into supertest 7.2.2's private `serverAddress` and `end`, which a version change can move, and the spec is what would say so. **Diagnostic rule:** an e2e status that fits no path its request could take is checked against this first, starting with whether the response carries `x-correlation-id`. CI is unlikely to meet it, a fresh runner having no desktop tool binding loopback ports, and the patch is harmless there | task 85, task 87, task 88 |

Chaining keeps a later `save` from overtaking an earlier one, which would leave the queue holding the snapshot from before the reporter's change. **What is not fixed, and cannot be by any page**: a transaction commits when it goes idle and IndexedDB offers no synchronous flush, so a renderer killed in that window still loses the write. This is assumed acceptable because the window is sub-millisecond and a real tab close runs the unload path; if that is wrong, UX-35's *queued* derives from the store's acknowledgement rather than the reducer's, which is a change to the indicator, not to the queue | FR-38, NFR-56, §4.10, UX-35, task 35.2 |

**`identity.admin_account` keeps its invariant that every row holds a password and a confirmed second factor**, because only the acceptance that sets both creates one. **The link lives 24 hours** and is single-use; a resend rotates the token and restarts the 24 hours on the same row — task 26.1's *one live link, ever* — and clears any staged secret, so a link superseded mid-enrolment leaves nothing behind. **Acceptance is A-20, over three bearer routes beside the handshake** (`/auth/admin/invitation/{preview,enrolment,acceptance}`, public to both guards, Origin-proven like the handshake's writes): the bearer of a live token reads what it invites; | Support access by the organization's consent, and the read a grant opens — task 67.9 | **Set 14 Sep 2026, project owner.** **(1) The organization consents** — an amendment to FR-78, UC-85 and UX-124: a Platform Administrator's request is only a request, **an active Organization Administrator of the named organization grants or declines it**, and nobody at the platform can grant on the organization's behalf. **(2) A live grant opens the organization's reports, read-only, scoped by RLS**: the api reads under the granted organization's tenant binding in a `READ ONLY` transaction as `esg_app`, so the same policies scope it as scope a member's read, and `esg_admin_ro`'s `BYPASSRLS` is not the path. **Each read is logged before it runs, and a failed log write refuses the read** — `admin-readonly.ts`'s stance, since FR-79's *what was accessed* is the condition of the access, not a record after it. **(3) A grant lasts 60 minutes, fixed, and is read-only, fixed**; a longer need is a new request with its own reason and its own grant. **(4) Any Platform Administrator may end any grant, and every Platform Administrator reads the whole log** — a privilege that needs restraining is restrained by peers. **(5) Any active Organization Administrator answers, from a banner across the signed-in tenant screens**; there is no email until the notification tasks (49 … 52), so a request is seen when an administrator next opens the application. **(6) A request nobody answers lapses after 24 hours.** **(7) While access lasts every member of the organization sees the banner** — the operator's address, the ticket, the reason and the time left — **and any Organization Administrator can end it**: consent that can be given can be withdrawn. **(8) A-08's support-access column counts each operator's requests in the last 30 days**, whatever became of them. **The lifecycle has no table of its own**, task 67.3's decision: `audit.support_access_log`'s `entry_kind` widens, a request and every decision against it — a grant, a decline, an end — are rows carrying the request's id, and the state is folded from them. **Nothing expires by a job**: *awaiting* lasts until a decision or 24 hours, *active* from a grant for 60 minutes unless ended, and both limits are the clock read against the rows — so FR-78's *without administrator action* holds with no worker and no row written at expiry, and the log shows *lapsed* and *expired* as derived states. **Four rules the build fixed.** **Consent is enforced by the log's policies, not by the api**: the insert policy an unbound connection meets admits an acquisition, a request, an access and a platform end and **never a grant or a decline**, and the organization's insert policy admits a grant, decline or end only for the bound organization, in the organization's realm, with the bound member as actor — so no defect above the database can answer for an organization; *which* member may answer (an Organization Administrator) is the route's role guard, since a policy cannot read a role without binding the membership table. The organization's select policy shows `esg_app` the bound organization's requests and answers and **never an acquisition or an access**. **A grant is the asking operator's alone to read under**, since the organization consents to the operator its banner names (decisions 1 and 7); any Platform Administrator may still end it (decision 4). **An operator holds at most one waiting or running request per organization**, and a second is refused (`support-access-outstanding`, 409) — a second banner from the same person is noise to the organization, and the first can be ended or left to lapse. **A-07's form names the organization from the register by id** (`GET /admin/organizations/{id}`), logged as A-02's page is, rather than from a name carried in the address. **The migration's `down` is lossy** — the grant half's rows cannot be held by the table it reverts to — and lifts `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` and the append-only trigger for its one DELETE, inside its transaction. |

The operator edits the enabled state, the client id, the issuer and the redirect addresses; **the requested scopes are shown and fixed at FR-2's three**, because FR-2 forbids a fourth and the flow cannot match or register without the identifier and the email. No deployment holds real accounts yet (tasks 71–72). **(4) The first password needs recent proof, since there is no current password to ask for**: a session created by a provider sign-in within the last 15 minutes, or — on the path where the provider did not assert the address — a confirmation link consumed within the last 15 minutes, which lands on the password step and signs the person in once the password is set. The link stays single-use and valid 24 hours; a stale session signs in at the provider again. **On the link path the password step asks whether to keep the person signed in on this device**, as S-01's credential form does, and the session takes the lifetime chosen — set 14 Sep 2026 by the owner at the task's parent-close review, since that step is a form that can carry the answer and OQ-35's reason for the provider's remembered default does not reach it. **(5) An invitee who registers through a provider completes both steps, then returns to the invitation** (UC-15). **(6) The names and language are saved by a setup-only call**, usable only in `awaiting_setup`; S-27's profile update is task 52.3's and separate. **(7) One new screen, S-36 *Complete your account*,** Focus archetype, a password step then a name-and-language step (`design_spec.md` §5.1). **(8) The password-reset email is worded for an account holding no password** — *set a password*, in three locales — rather than telling it its current password stays unchanged. **So is the page that link opens**: S-02's set-password step reads *set a password*, not *set a new password* — set 14 Sep 2026 by the owner at the task's parent-close review. The setup email's link names the wording, and a link that does not reads as a reset, so every link sent before this lands keeps its meaning. **A password reset admits an account in `awaiting_setup` as well as an active one** — (8)'s wording reaches nobody otherwise, and an account in setup whose provider is disabled on A-18 would have no way back (FR-82); a reset sets the password half of setup and leaves the name step to S-36. **Implementation (task 155.1).** The gate is `AuthGuard`'s, from the account's status and deadline now read with the session: an account in setup meets `account-setup-required` on every session-bearing route not marked `@AdmitsAccountInSetup`, and one past its deadline is no account (`authentication-required`); public routes — sign-out and refresh among them — never reach the check. The deadline is `identity.account.setup_expires_at`. The setup routes are `identity/provider`'s, FR-2's module and already the issuer of provider sessions: `GET /account/setup` (what S-36 renders from — address, stored name parts, language, whether a password is held), `POST /account/setup/password`, `POST /account/setup/profile`, and the public `POST /auth/account-setup/password` for the link path. **The provider-sign-in proof needs no new column**: an account holding no password can hold no session but a provider sign-in's — password sign-in needs a credential, and refresh keeps `identity.session.created_at` — so the session's own creation instant is the proof. **The link's grant is a password-reset token with a 15-minute life**, minted by `POST /auth/verify-email` for an account holding no password and returned in its body: it is the same exchange of proven mailbox control for a credential, so it reuses that table's single-use claim rather than adding a fourth token kind. Activation is judged on what the account holds — a password and both name parts — whichever route put them there, and the reset email carries `holdsPassword` so the worker picks (8)'s wording. **Settled at the parent-close review.** The grant is kept apart from an emailed reset link by the token row's `purpose` — `reset` or `account_setup` — and each route claims only its own, so a link from UC-08 never signs anyone in and a grant never reaches the reset route; consuming a grant revokes every session the account already held before issuing its own, FR-6's rule for a consumed reset token, under the reset's own reason `password_reset` since the grant is one. The session path revokes nothing: its proof is the session itself, and no link was consumed. Both routes look the token up before hashing the password, so a public request presenting an unknown value costs an indexed read rather than an Argon2id derivation, while the claim inside the transaction still decides single use. Refresh ends a setup past its deadline, the account being no account (OQ-52). The confirmation's answer carries the grant's expiry, which the web tier's sealed cookie takes rather than restating the quarter-hour; and the setup email's link carries `intent=setup`, which only chooses S-02's wording — the token alone decides what consuming it does. |

| The browser suite stops the dev servers, then starts its own — task 102 | **Set 16 Sep 2026, project owner.** The suite served the stack on the ports the developer's own servers use — api 3000, web 3100, console 3200 — with `reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI`, and Playwright 1.62.1 decides a server is running when its `url` answers and records the reuse only under `DEBUG=pw:webserver`. So a local run could test whatever answered, a `next dev` or a stale orphan, and say nothing. The principle: **what is tested is the build that ships, differing only in its environment**; so the remedy is to *stop the dev servers before the suite starts*, not to give the suite ports of its own, which would need a second console build because the api's address is inlined by Vite. **(1) The suite keeps the dev ports**, declared once in `e2e/stack.ts` and read by the config, the specs and the stop script — so the console is built once, by `pree2e:web`. **(2) `tools/stop-dev-servers.mjs` runs first in `pree2e:web`**, before the builds: for each of the suite's ports it finds the listening process and, **only when that process runs from this repository** (its working directory), stops its whole process group — what Ctrl+C does to a terminal job — waiting for the port to free and escalating to `SIGKILL` if it does not. The unit is the group because stopping only the port's process leaves `nest start --watch` alive to restart the api on the next edit. **A process from anywhere else is never touched** — 3000 is a common default and the port may belong to another project — and the run fails naming it. Skipped when `CI` is set, where a runner starts with nothing listening. **(3) `reuseExistingServer: false` on every server entry stays as the backstop**: anything that starts on one of those ports between the stop and the suite's own start fails the run at start rather than being adopted. **(4) Every origin the stack reads about itself is set explicitly** — the web app's `PUBLIC_WEB_URL`, which `social-flow.ts` redirects through, per server, and the api's — rather than left to defaults that are right only because the suite listens on the dev ports. **Declined**: ports of the suite's own (a second console build); keeping reuse with a build-identity check (a test concern in two apps); and closing §18's deferred console-address question with a serve-time setting, which is more than this task needs — that row's assumption, one build per environment, stands. **Cost**: `pnpm e2e:web` and `pnpm gates` stop this repository's dev servers, and the developer starts them again afterwards | tasks 23, 30.2, 92, 113, OQ-17 |

What this does **not** see is an asynchronous bounce — accepted, then rejected hours later — which over SMTP returns as a DSN to the sender mailbox and would need IMAP; and **complaints are out of reach entirely**, since a feedback loop is an ESP relationship. The seam where an ESP's webhook lands is the adapter, and it is the only thing that changes when one is configured. **(2) Suppression is platform-wide**, one row per normalised address in `notification.suppressed_address` — a bounce is a property of the mailbox, not of the tenant, and suppressing per organization would leave every other organization writing to a mailbox already known to be gone. SELECT` in the run's transaction so what it retains is what the table held; §7.2's `CALC_RUN → CALC_INPUT` keeps its meaning and `CALC_SOURCE` is added. **Declined**: inputs owned by a draft run that commit freezes (§7.2's diagram read literally), which restarts a line's field history at every commit, and a run per keystroke. A run is recorded on request (`POST /reports/{id}/calculator/runs`); 38.4 gives it results and the write into B3. **(2) A line's site is the report's own B1 site row**, its ordinal on `IdentifierOfSiteTypedAxis` — a row being any ordinal a site-axis element is stored at, plus one per site the period's snapshot holds, the wizard's own rule — so the calculator sums over the sites the report discloses (FR-19). **Declined**: `core.site`, the entity's live record, which moves after the period opens and holds no consolidated subsidiary's site; and a free-text name. **A B1 site holding lines cannot be removed until its lines are**, and today that holds because nothing removes a site row at all — `DisclosureValueStore.remove` has no product caller, and a cleared value keeps its row — so **the task that adds row removal inherits the refusal**. **(3) A line holds one figure for the period; the artboard's monthly form is deferred to task 39.1**, with its shape stated: twelve month rows under the line whose sum becomes its quantity, an expand-only migration, and a run's copy carrying the quantity either way. Assumed meanwhile: a reporter with monthly bills totals them before entering. **Taken in the build, and stated:** a line's id is chosen by its client and keyed `(organization_id, id)`, so FR-38's replayed autosave writes the same line and no tenant's id can meet another's; the upsert updates only a line of the same report, refusing a move between reports. The factor set is the organization's country's (`core.organization.country_code`), a site's own grid country being a later concern — what changes if a non-Moldovan site enters scope is that a run pins one set per country. A line's source and unit are checked against the set the period resolves when written, and every copied line again against the set the run pins, so a correction that dropped a source refuses the run rather than recording an input nothing can evaluate; a run over no lines is refused, *"zero is an answer someone might file"*. **The run tables are immutable by grant and permanent by key**: `esg_app` holds `SELECT` and `INSERT` only, neither carries an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` policy, and their keys into `core.report` take no `ON DELETE` action, so OQ-20's *CALC_INPUT permanent* makes a report a run rests on undeletable — the organization-lapse work (65.2, 163) inherits that. `recorded_by` is the request's own `app.current_user` binding, as `core.field_change` attributes | AD-2, AD-14, DR-4, FR-19, FR-33, FR-35, NFR-19, OQ-20, P-11, UX-34, UX-41 |
| Scope 1 computed exactly, and absent rather than zero — task 38.2 | **Taken in the build, 1 Oct 2026**, within FR-34 and NFR-19; no source was silent on a question it needed answered. **(1) The arithmetic is exact** — decimal strings multiplied and summed as `bigint`s scaled by a power of ten (`contracts/types/decimal.ts`, moved there by task 38.4), with no library. A figure is `quantity × MWh per unit × tCO₂e per MWh`, summed over lines, and products and sums of finite decimals are finite, so no intermediate is rounded or lost; floats would put binary noise into a filed figure's last places (`500 × 0.0095773` is `4.7886500000000005`). NFR-19's *exact reproduction* is then a property of the numbers rather than of the runtime. `derivation.model.ts`'s rates stay floats: they divide, which exactness cannot survive, and the GHG intensity (38.4) meets the same limit and will need its own stated rule. **No rounding**: the unrounded total is kept, and a figure is rounded once at presentation (S-09's artboard). **(2) A scope with no measured line has no total, not zero** — FR-30's distinction: zero is a nil return someone files, and a calculator holding no fuel line has not said the company burns none. A scope whose lines are all explained is the same case; one partly explained totals the measured lines and lists the rest, the artboard's *"one site of two"*. **(3) What makes a source Scope 1 is the factor set's `ghgScope`**, never a list of fuels in code, so a source registered as data is counted with no release. **For 38.3**: task 37 put the grid factor in the same set and the same window as the fuels, so 38.3 is the location-based scope over `scope-total.ts`, not a second factor path | FR-30, FR-34, NFR-19, §7.9 |

The intensity sums its scopes rather than reading the derived total, because a derivation is recomputed in one pass over stored operands. **(2) The intensity is stored to ten significant figures, half-up** — the one division in the calculator, so the one rounding; scale-free, since tCO₂e per leu is ~0.0000004; no turnover or a zero one is no intensity.
