| Billing catalogue and subscription, settled where the requirements were restated — task 182 | **Set 5 Oct 2026, project owner.** These settle twenty-four points that FR-84 … FR-113 (`functional_requirements/06-commercial.md`) left undecided, numbered 182/57 … 182/80. **(182/57) Free is the absence of a subscription.** An organization with no billing record is on Free and holds the entitlements of the Free plan's currently published version; a record appears at the first trial or the first order, and an organization holds at most one subscription in force. *Lapsed* now means a subscription that ended, never an organization that was always on Free. The reason: founding is a core act and the core cannot write the `billing` schema (DR-1), and with `BILLING_ENABLED=false` there is no record to hold. A consequence: Free carries no version pin, so a new Free version applies to every organization without a subscription from its publication, and grandfathering is for subscriptions only. If Free were to be pinned, every organization would need a subscription from founding and this decision reverses. **(182/58) The six states**, read off UC-103, UC-104, UC-141 and UC-142: *trialling*, a trial running; *active*, a paid period in force; *past due*, a renewal charge or an invoice overdue with dunning running; *suspended*, dunning exhausted; *cancelled*, cancellation requested with service continuing to the period's end; *lapsed*, ended and now on Free. FR-90 item 7 lists the transitions. A trial that is not converted is read as lapsed, because UC-95 calls its end a lapse to Free, although the owner's wording in 182/57 says *paid*; if a trial's end should leave another record, FR-90 item 6 changes. **(182/59) Plan versions, entitlements, prices and discounts are tables in the `billing` schema, not configuration-store artefacts** (project owner). Each plan version has its own published or retired state and is published under UX-123. §4.5, DR-3 and AD-4 are amended to agree with §6.4, §7.4 and §7.10. Consequences: a subscription references an exact version inside one schema; a published version stays immutable, the property AD-4 gave the store, now kept on the tables; the store keeps plan *presentation* copy only (FR-61, task 53.3); §7.5 no longer lists plan prices as effective-dated; tasks 53, 53.1, 53.2, 81.1 and 120.1 lose their `config` scope. Assumed meanwhile: a plan version has no effective-from date of its own, so what is on sale is what is published. If a scheduled future price is wanted, a published-from date is added to the version. **(182/60) Publication attaches to a plan version, retirement to the plan** and closes every version to new sales; a plan returns to sale only by publishing a new version. Prices and trial terms are per version, so what is on sale is a version, and retiring a plan must close all of them. **(182/61) The order's transitions:** draft to awaiting payment on confirmation; awaiting payment to paid on settlement; paid to provisioned when the entitlements are applied; awaiting payment to expired when the proforma's validity ends; draft or awaiting payment to cancelled; awaiting payment to failed on a hard decline or a provider failure. `inconsistent` is the saga's status beside the order, not an eighth state, so the customer sees seven and the residue stays the operator's (A-10, NFR-59). The expiry period is configuration (AD-4), tied to the proforma's validity date, and its value is set with the saga (58.1); no source fixes it. **(182/62) An order is cancellable while unpaid, whether or not a payment is in flight;** unpaid is draft or awaiting payment. A payment arriving afterwards goes to reconciliation as an unmatched payment (FR-133). On the transfer rail what is in flight cannot be known, and FR-133 already covers money that arrives for a cancelled order. **(182/63) At a trial's expiry**, where the terms require an instrument and recurring consent was recorded, conversion creates an order and charges the stored instrument (FR-120); otherwise the Administrator must confirm an order and the trial lapses to Free if not confirmed. It follows UX-60 and BR-PAY-5, no charge without recorded consent. **(182/64) A new export from a read-only report is blocked only on suspension** (UC-142). After a downgrade such reports stay exportable within Free's export entitlement, so UC-101 gains no block and BR-ENT-2 remains a quota rule. **(182/65) "Most recently active"** is the latest field change on a report, which the change trail holds; an entity's activity is the latest over its reports; ties go to the earlier-created; the number retained is the reduced entitlement's ceiling; the rule is published as a help-centre article and restated in the consequence dialogue. Reads are not activity, since no access record exists. **(182/66) Currencies:** every priced plan version carries an MDL price, EUR and USD are optional, and the customer picks the order's currency among those the version is priced in. MDL stays the ledger currency (D-14), and the rate for a foreign-currency invoice is FR-129's. **(182/67) Inline comparatives are free on every plan.** D-12's *comparative-period features* is the deferred standalone view (FR-179). No key is added, and task 54.2 enumerates no comparatives seam; the prior-period read stays ungated. **(182/68) Entitlement keys are data:** names follow the dotted pattern and are settled in task 53.2's batch, and a key holds a switch, a ceiling or a tier. `ENTITLEMENT_KEYS` in `entitlement.port.ts` is deleted by task 54.1, and AD-5's *registered in configuration* now reads *registered as catalogue data*. **(182/69) "Immediately" for an upgrade means at the confirmed payment of the upgrade order,** the credit already netted in its total. BR-SUB-1 says nothing changes on order creation, and on the transfer rail the upgrade waits for settlement and the screen says so. **(182/70) "Approaching" is a warning band, data on the entitlement,** defaulting to one unit remaining, which is the S-16 precedent; `allow_with_warning` is returned inside it. A percentage means nothing for a ceiling of ten seats, and the numbers per key are set in task 53.2. **(182/71) One trial per organization, ever, started from Free only** (amended 6 Oct 2026, project owner). Without a limit a trial is a standing free upgrade. An organization that has started any trial — of any plan, whether it lapsed, converted or was cancelled — cannot start another, **and S-18 does not render the start-a-trial control for it, nor for an organization on a paid plan**: the refusals stay the server's, and the screen simply never offers them. **(182/72) Proration is daily:** the remaining whole days over the period's days, rounded half-up to minor units, the credit offsetting the new charge only, with no cash refund. **(182/73) No MVP plan prices a unit,** so FR-96 is specified and dormant and an order's quantity is 1. Fixing a unit price remains the owner's OQ-8 decision and is not pre-empted. **(182/74) Reactivation has no window, and organization life ends only when the organization record is deleted.** UC-105's retention-window precondition is struck; DD-13 deletes nothing on a lapse, so a window nothing closes would have no effect, and a lapse or suspension never ends organization life, which fixes NFR-109's retention anchor. Task 163 keeps the unknowns of the deletion itself. **(182/75) Three cases, three routes:** withdrawing a cancellation before the period ends needs no payment; a lapsed subscription is bought again through an order on a published plan; a suspended one is restored by paying the overdue amount (UC-143). **(182/76) The subscription history records every state-changing transition,** the system being the actor for what it does (renewal, lapse, suspension, restoration). The six classes of UC-107 are its first members and not its limit, because a dispute about a suspension is the likeliest one. **(182/77) A discount is validated at entry, reserved at confirmation, consumed at paid and released on cancelled, expired or failed; one code per order.** Consuming at entry would let an abandoned draft exhaust a limited code, and consuming at paid alone would let two buyers take the last redemption. **(182/78) A recurring discount applies in every period until the subscription leaves the plan version it was applied to;** a fixed amount is authored per currency, like a price (D-14). **(182/79) "Reports per period" counts reports in total for the organization,** not per fiscal year and not per billing cycle (project owner), and the entitlement wording is renamed *reports in total* throughout. Two consequences are assumed, not decided. A report deleted under FR-210 no longer counts, having left every list and route. And because metering events are kept 24 months, a lifetime total cannot be summed from them, so task 62.3 holds the reports counter as a maintained count. If deleted reports should keep their slot, or the counter should stay event-derived, FR-85 item 6 and FR-105 item 9 change. **(182/80) At renewal a subscriber on a retired plan moves to the successor the Operator named when retiring the plan** (project owner; declined: leaving subscribers on the retired version). Retiring therefore requires naming a successor, assumed to be a plan on sale, and the move is disclosed before it happens: on S-24 from the retirement, and by a notice whose category and lead time are set by the task that registers it. This amends BR-SUB-6, whose sentence *terminates no existing service* now reads: service continues without a gap, on the successor. **Build work** is five new rows: 54.5 (an organization with no subscription), 53.4 (publishing and retiring plan versions), 60.5 (renewal onto the successor), 58.4 (order expiry) and 60.6 (trial eligibility and conversion). Rows 53, 53.1, 53.2, 54.1, 54.2, 58.1, 62.3, 63.2, 63.8 … 63.10, 68.2, 68.3, 81.1, 81.2 and 120.1 are amended to match. |
| Payment, invoicing, reconciliation, collections and Enterprise billing, settled where the requirements were restated — task 182 | **Set 5 Oct 2026, project owner**, numbered 182/81 … 182/114. These settle thirty-four points that FR-114 … FR-152 and FR-106, FR-107 (parts 6 and 7 of `functional_requirements/`) left undecided. Twelve rest on a fact only an outside party holds — the statutory fiscal year, the document language, the e-Factura specification, the archive form, the bank, the acquirer, the accountant, the settlement reports — and were accepted as stated assumptions; each says below what changes if it is wrong, and 55.4 and 193 exist to replace them with answers. **182/81 Approved bank transfer terms are an Enterprise property recorded on the contract** (FR-144, FR-145): the invoice is issued at a scheduled billing point before payment and entitlements follow at issuance. On the self-serve transfer rail there are none: the proforma and its order are the open document, the fiscal invoice is issued when the match confirms payment, and entitlements follow reconciliation (BR-PAY-4). This makes FR-92, BR-SUB-1, BR-PAY-4 and FR-122 true together without an approval workflow no actor row describes, and puts the only pre-payment invoices where DD-12 and FR-147 already put them. **182/82 Recurring consent is a field of the stored instrument and goes with it**: replace is add-with-new-consent then remove, a replacement never inherits consent, removal withdraws it. The entity row already put the consent record inside the instrument, and UX-60 asks for each recurring authorisation to be an explicit act. **182/83 A subscription with no stored card is renewed by an order created at a configured lead time** — a proforma on transfer, a request-to-pay on MIA, the rail last used — with a notice; the lead time is 14 days (project owner, 5 Oct 2026, starting-values row). Non-card renewal is most paying customers (DD-8 makes transfer the default for annual billing), so lapsing them or requiring a card would be wrong. Task 60.7 builds it. **182/84 Three document types — invoice, credit note, corrective invoice — each have a series**, a number printing as series code, fiscal year and running integer; a credit note answers a refund or a cancellation and a corrective invoice a genuine error; **the fiscal year is the calendar year in `Europe/Chisinau`, a stated assumption**. AD-7 already keys the counter on type, series and year. If the statutory rule differs, only the derivation of the year and the roll date change, and issued documents keep their year. **182/85 All three VAT treatments are defined now** (project owner; declined: shipping the domestic rule alone): domestic supply at the standard rate when the billing account's legal-address country is Moldova; export at zero when it is not and no VAT registration code is held; reverse charge, no VAT charged, when it is not and a code is held. **Residency is derived from the legal-address country and held nowhere else.** Rates, rules and basis wording are rows of the `vat_rule` artefact. At the MVP every customer is domestic (DD-9), so the other two rows are exercised by test data until the merchant-of-record rail is activated. **The selection rules, the zero rate and the basis meanings are a stated assumption pending a tax adviser (55.4)**; if wrong, rows change as data and no code does. **182/86 The fiscal document is printed in Romanian only**, rendered once at issuance and stored with its XML, so the delivered and the archived document are identical; the covering email is in the recipient's locale; the customer receives and downloads the PDF and the XML is the transmitted record read in A-12. The statutory-language rule is an external fact held as an assumption; if it differs, only the template catalogue and the rendering step change, and issued documents stay as issued. **182/87 e-Factura's format, transport and timing are a verification task before 56.1** (55.4); meanwhile every issued invoice and every corrective document is assumed in scope, the transport direct, transmission immediate from the outbox with retry. The mandate has been in effect since 1 October 2026. If the specification differs, only the adapter behind `EInvoicingPort` and its configuration change (NFR-14). **182/88 Reissue is by cause**: an outage or a platform-side schema failure retransmits the same document under its number; a data cause cancels by credit note and issues a new invoice referencing it. The assumption is that e-Factura does not register a rejected document; if it does, retransmission is dropped and every cause takes the credit-note path, losing only the property that an outage heals without consuming a number. **182/89 The statutory form is the transmitted XML, the acknowledgement and the rendered document, archived together at acknowledgement**, retention six years from the end of the fiscal year of issue, retrieval by a runbook against the bucket (73.7); at expiry the lock lapses and no deletion path is built. The form and the start of retention are an external fact held as an assumption; if they differ, only the archive writer's trigger and contents change. **182/90 Reconciliation resolutions are a closed set of four** — apply, apply in part, refund through FR-139, reject — admitted per exception class; a partial payment leaves the invoice open for the balance; whoever claims an exception owns it. A closed set lets the ledger entry say what happened and keeps refunds inside FR-139's authority rule. **182/91 Dunning attaches to the unpaid renewal order**, due on the renewal date, **or to an invoice issued before payment** under approved terms; no fiscal invoice is issued for an unpaid card renewal. Issuing one would create an irreversible document that may never be paid, contradicting FR-122 and D-10. UC-123's second step and UC-141's precondition are amended. **182/92 A-11's suspend and restore are Billing Operator exceptions** with a rationale, written to the ledger as an entitlement-override entry; **restoration is automatic once no overdue amount remains, by any settlement route**, and a partial settlement does not restore. **182/93 Issuing corrections and refunding are two permissions** that no Billing Operator account holds together, directly or through its roles (the role model of 182/3). Issuing is otherwise the system's act, so the permission governs the Operator's hand-issued credit note or corrective invoice; the credit note a refund generates needs neither. This is the reading under which FR-139's third criterion is testable; maker-checker would add a workflow no source asks for. Task 66.4. **182/94 Card refunds go to origin through the acquirer adapter; a transfer refund is made from the company's own bank, outside the platform**, recorded with its bank reference, total capped at the amount paid, the credit note generated on recorded completion. A MIA payment is assumed to be refunded by transfer; if its adapter can refund to origin, the adapter declares it and nothing else moves. **182/95 Acceptance of an Enterprise quote is the Operator recording the executed contract against it**; the quote is then read-only and provisioning is from the contract, pre-filled from the quote. An opportunity is requested, quoted or concluded and may be closed with a reason; a quote is draft, issued, accepted or expired. **182/96 The MIA ceiling is compared with the order's gross total in MDL, per transaction only**; the cumulative figure is held as data and not enforced, because the daily limit is the payer's bank's and cannot be observed. **182/97 The payment reference is an opaque per-order code with a check character, unique across the platform**, and the proforma names the platform's own receiving account(s) from configuration. The check character lets the matcher tell a typo from a stranger's payment (FR-133); a reference derived from a document number is unavailable because a proforma consumes none. **182/98 The soft-decline schedule is a configuration artefact beside the dunning sequence**; each acquirer adapter classifies its results soft or hard; the failure notice's deadline is the date dunning would restrict service. One clock governs BR-PAY-6 and FR-135. The schedule is days 1, 3 and 7 (project owner, 5 Oct 2026, starting-values row). **182/99 A day with no rate takes the last rate published on or before the invoice date**, with that rate's own date stored; an unreachable source makes issuance wait and consumes no number, which keeps AD-7's rule that a number is consumed only on issuance. **182/100 One statement file format is accepted first — that of the bank holding the operating account**; a line is identified by bank reference, date and amount so re-import adds nothing; the bank-API pull is deferred. Which bank is the owner's fact (193); if its format is not file-based, only the importer changes. **182/101 A confident match needs the reference, the amount and the payer's fiscal code exactly equal and one candidate**; anything else is an exception. The conservative reading of a financial assertion: widening later is easy, and narrowing after a wrong settlement is not. **182/102 The dunning reminder is transactional and goes to every Organization Administrator**; the default sequence — steps, offsets, grace — is reminders at +1, +7 and +14 days and restriction at +21 (project owner, 5 Oct 2026, starting-values row). A reminder that warns of restriction has the same stakes as UC-125's failure notice. If the owner prefers an optional reminder, only its classification changes. **182/103 Write-off treatments are a closed list the company's accountant supplies**, held as configuration; a write-off leaves the subscription's state alone and is superseded, not reversed, if the debt is later paid. The treatment feeds the accountant's books (FR-150), so the platform does not invent categories. **182/104 The chargeback evidence pack is a bundle the Operator downloads and submits through the acquirer's channel**; the outcome, won or lost, is entered by hand; a lost case triggers FR-125's correction and FR-141. No source gives the acquirer a dispute API. Formats, outcome values and deadlines are the acquirer's and held as an assumption (193); an API would make submission additive. **182/105 The Operator chooses at refund time how the subscription is treated** — no change, read-only now, read-only from period close — and the choice is recorded with the refund; the three cases are exactly those whose answer is a commercial judgement. **182/106 Contract terms are structured only where billing acts on them**: term, notice period, price-protection cap and period. The SLA and non-standard clauses are text with an attached document; the purchase-order reference is length-bounded text (64 characters, a routine value to reconcile with the e-Factura buyer-reference field). Entitlement overrides last for the contract term and carry no window of their own; one is additive if a ramp-up is ever sold. **182/107 A billing schedule is a list of dated billing points on the contract**, each with an issue date and a due date; a milestone point is undated and released by the Operator with a rationale; approaching expiry is surfaced at a configured lead time before the notice date. Dated points express all four shapes without a recurrence language; the lead time is the owner's. **182/108 The dashboard's measures are defined by the company's accountant**, with the recorded draft as the starting point; the measures are seven, and the index criterion's count of six is corrected to match its text. A revenue figure the accountant disputes is worse than a late one; until the definitions arrive no definition binds the build. **182/109 The accountant export is one file per document set plus a VAT summary, for a period the Operator chooses**, with MDL equivalents; a period is closed when it has ended and nothing paid in it awaits invoicing. The file format is fixed when the accountant states what the return needs; if the return needs a fixed layout, only the export's columns change. **182/110 Each ledger entry is written by the use case that causes the event, in its own transaction**, holding event class, actor, timestamp, subject reference and amount in minor units; the system writes the superseding entry on a compensating event, and the console offers no supersede action, since no source gives it one. **182/111 Settlement reconciliation: each rail adapter parses its provider's report to one common line shape and matches on the acquirer's transaction reference**; tolerance, timing window and agreed fee are configuration set after the first real report from each provider is seen (193); none is assumed. **182/112 The billing account holds exactly FR-106's five fields**, the contact being a name and an email; the legal name, IDNO, legal address and contact email are required before an order and the VAT code is optional; no e-Factura recipient is held, and S-15's mention of one is struck. The legal address includes its country, which 182/85 reads. | A factor set validated at publication, and the report-update notice when one is replaced — tasks 37.3, 37.4 | **Set 6 Oct 2026, project owner.** **(1) Publication validates a payload by its kind, and refuses a factor set with any malformed source** (37.4; 182/50). `ConfigurationPublisher.publish` asks the kind's rule before it writes anything, and `emission_factor_set`'s rule is the reader's own, `readFactorSetPayload`: a set the reader rejects whole is refused, and so is one it would read **with a source dropped** — the reader drops a malformed source so a run is refused for that source alone, but at publication someone is present to correct it, and a dropped source is one no reporter can calculate. Refused, publishing nothing, by `ConfigurationPayloadRefusedError`, which names the reason; **the 400 `validation-failed` is the mapping of the screen that publishes**, as A-18's store maps a revision mismatch onto its own refusal — the store is generic and knows no problem type, and no route publishes a factor set until A-05 (task 67.8). **It holds for the seed loader too**, so a malformed seed fails `config:seed` rather than reaching a run. A revert is not validated: it restores a version already published, and NFR-85 wants it to be one step under pressure. **(2) A factor set is replaced when the revision in force for its slot changes** — a publication over an occupied window, or a revert — and the revision leaving is the one replaced; a publication into an empty window, a later year's set, replaces nothing. The publisher writes a platform outbox event, `calculator.factor_set_replaced` (country, leaving, entering), on the publication's own transaction (P-8), so the seed, a revert and A-05 later all reach the notice by one path. **(3) An organization is affected when an open report's latest run is pinned to the revision leaving.** A locked, ready-to-file or filed report cannot be recalculated (FR-22, FR-73), and an earlier run of a report is history rather than its figure. *Amended 12 Oct 2026* (§12.5.6's task-47 row (2)): only the lock refuses a recalculation — a filed report in an open period is open, and is affected. **(4) The worker finds the organizations by a policy of its own on `core.calc_run`**, `calc_run_worker_directory_select`, a `SELECT` for `esg_worker` that holds only while no organization is bound — task 25.3's directory precedent of visibility conditioned on the unbound state, so a bound job sees exactly its tenant. | The validation rule definition and its interpreter — task 40 | **Set 7 Oct 2026, project owner.** Each kind below is one of the checks the EFRAG template makes (`config/efrag/1.3.0/VSME-Digital-Template-1.3.0.xlsx`, the *Table of Contents & Validation* sheet and the status columns). **(1) A closed vocabulary of eight rule kinds: a new rule is data, a new kind is code.** `required` — each field it names is answered, and a presence rule may hold only *when* another answer does (that answer given, or a yes/no answered yes: B4's link only when the disclosure is public); `required_any` — at least one of several; `row_complete` — a row of a list, once started, is finished, every element the rule names answered at that member or position; `sum` — weighted parts against a total, *equal*, *at most* or *at least*, so the calculation linkbase's weighted arcs and the template's one-sided checks both fit; `range` — a number within an inclusive minimum and maximum, non-negativity being a minimum of zero; `url` — the address form, (4); `exclusive` — an answer that leaves other elements empty, such as a disclosure published elsewhere and the same table also filled in; and `year_over_year` — 182/28's one proportion, at most one per set, flagging a movement **beyond** it (strictly greater) against a comparable prior at the same natural key (FR-45, FR-46 item 3). A field is named by its element and, optionally, an axis member; with no member it means every row the element holds. **A rule naming any element outside the evaluation's scope is not evaluated**, and the caller states the scope: the elements the report's pinned version holds, that apply (FR-28's thresholds artefact, which the api evaluates, §9.8) and whose module is not declared omitted (FR-31) *(and since task 210 the fields the reporting entity's record answers — the task-210 row (1), (g))*. AD-10's *a BullMQ queue* is amended to say so, and the rule that there is exactly one `@Processor` becomes one per queue. *Declined:* one queue with a higher consumer concurrency, which a burst as large as the concurrency, or as many hung renders, blocks again; one queue with a lower priority for exports, under which a waiting email still waits for the export already running — up to the 60 s deadline on a hang. **What the building settled, under those five.** *(a) What Chromium tags, measured* on 151 against veraPDF: headings, lists, tables with header scope and cell headers, `/Lang` and the displayed title are its own; the output intent and identification XMP, a body for each list item, a description for each link and the Artifact marking of what is drawn but is not content are not, and the finisher (`apps/renderer/finisher/finish_pdf.py`) adds exactly those. **It refuses rather than guesses**: untagged text inside the page body, or links that do not pair one to one with the document's anchors, fail the render instead of being hidden or mislabelled. OQ-7 closes. *(b) An empty table cell cannot be tagged* — Chromium tags no cell with nothing painted in it, and a row a cell short fails PDF/UA-1 — so a figure with no unit prints a dash in the unit column, as the prior period's column already does. *(c) The page furniture is CSS page-margin boxes over named pages* (UX-118, the artboard's body pages): the undertaking and the report on the left of the header, the section on the right, carried onto a module's continuation pages; the standard's version, the scope and the language left of the footer, *Page n of m* right; none on the cover. It lives in the margins alone, so the preview — the same markup, with no margins on screen — shows none of it, and the finisher marks it as pagination by where it stands: inside the 20 mm the stylesheet's `@page` gives the margin. *(d) The file's own facts* (NFR-22; task-43 row (c)): the person who asked, by UX-137's name, and the moment the attempt began — on the cover and the provenance, and as the XMP's dates. **The moment is printed in the zone of the report's period, the zone named beside it — a recorded assumption**: no source says which zone a generation moment is printed in, and the period's is the one every date in the document already stands in. *(e) Whose words the labels are* is read from the label resolver at the report's pinned version (`standing`), never from a list of locales, and stated on the cover and the provenance in every language — EFRAG's own in English, the platform's translation in Romanian and Russian at `2026-05-01` (44.7; UX-98). *(f) The record, `core.export_artifact`*: what a request cannot say the database writes — a `BEFORE INSERT` stamp takes the requester from `app.current_user` and the template and taxonomy versions from the report, and the application is granted the four columns a request states; the worker settles a row by column, and the update policy admits a row only while it is `requested`, so a settled record takes no further write, its owner's included (FR-53 AC-2). Exempt from the lock and from field audit, as validation's runs are. *(g) The worker reads its organization*: `core.organization`'s invitation-bearer policy read `identity.invitation`, which `esg_worker` cannot, and PostgreSQL checks every table any applicable policy names — so the worker could read no organization at all. The policy is scoped `TO esg_app`: a role named on a *permissive* policy fails closed, which is why §7.6's `TO PUBLIC` reasoning does not reach it. *(h) The kill does not wait for Playwright*: a Chromium that hangs while launching never yields a handle, so each render's browser carries a switch naming the render, and the deadline sends `SIGKILL` to the process group of whatever carries it; a failure arriving after the deadline is answered as the deadline, once the kill is done. **The hang is made from outside**: the export suite stops the real browser with `SIGSTOP` through `docker exec`, and the shipped renderer knows nothing of tests. The container runs with an init process, as PostgreSQL's does (§12.5.10), so killed renders leave no zombies. *(i) A job's queue and retry are its handler's* (`@OnQueue`, `@RetriesWith`), read by `JobPlacement` for the dispatcher; a job takes AD-10's queue and the delivery retry where it declares neither, and a handler learns how many attempts it is given, so the last records the failure. *(j) One composition*: `ComposeReportDocument` reads the document's model in both modes — the preview renders it, the export's job prints it — so the report's store and the latest calculator run are now registered on the worker too. *(k) The stacks*: the renderer and the S3 emulator are in both Compose stacks — the renderer capped at 512 MB (a full report peaked at about 490 MB on Chromium 151, and one rendered under a 384 MB cap) — and veraPDF is a test-stack service under a profile of its own. CI builds the renderer once per stack job from the images job's cache, and the images job has the image print a document. *(l) The export suite is the regression suite* NFR-82 names: every file it produces is read by veraPDF against both profiles and by PDF.js for its words. | FR-49, FR-53, NFR-22, NFR-37, NFR-42, NFR-46, NFR-82, NFR-106, UX-46, UX-120, AD-10, T-13, OQ-7, §5, §12.5.9, §12.5.10, §15.3, tasks 15, 44, 47 |

| A disclosure field's help describes its control — task 241 | **Set 16 Nov 2026, project owner**, raised by task 79.2's journey (its build-log entry), where C2's narrative was described by its character count alone. **(1) The anatomy exposes the ids, and the caller wires them** (UX-17, UX-110): `DisclosureField` takes `helpId` and `messageId` beside `labelId`, auto-generated if omitted, and puts them on the help's and the message's elements; the slot's control points `aria-describedby` at them, as it already points `aria-labelledby` at `labelId`. `Select`, `RadioGroup` and `Combobox` gain `describedBy`, named ids appended after their own help and error — the text controls already merged a passed `aria-describedby` — and in `apps/web` `NumberField`, `ChoiceSet` and `DisclosureControl` pass it on, so every writable kind's control is described: text, year, narrative, date, number, the option cards, the long choice and the set. A read-only field and a computed figure draw no control, and nothing is wired there. *Declined:* a context the controls read, which would teach every generic form control the disclosure anatomy and make the anatomy a client boundary that the marketing home's Server Components render; `aria-describedby` on the field's group, which leaves the control's own description empty and is read inconsistently by screen readers on entry. **(2) The message is described too, after the help**: a reader arriving at a field hears its finding, its not-available reason or its carried note, as `TextField` speaks its error (WCAG 2.2 3.3.1). Its id is named only while a message shows, since its element exists only then. `role="status"` stays — it announces a change, and the description is what is read on focus. A carried note's *Confirm* button reads as words in the description, the accepted cost. A narrative's order is its count, then the help, then the message: `TextArea` puts a passed description after its own, unchanged here. |
| Every browser journey reads the console — task 243 | **Set 16 Nov 2026**, from the project owner's brief after commit 1abb3821, which found S-09 failing to hydrate on every load from task 39 under a green browser suite. **(1) One `test` for every journey, and a lint rule that keeps it so.** `e2e/support/test.ts` extends Playwright's `test` with an automatic fixture that listens to every context the journey opens — the `context` fixture's, and any `browser.newContext()` a spec makes, by wrapping that method for the test's length — for `weberror` and for console messages at `error`, and fails the journey after it ran, naming a hydration failure (React's production codes #418, #419, #423, #425, or the development build's sentence) as one. A fixture is automatic only for a spec that imports it, so `eslint.config.mjs` refuses `test` from `@playwright/test` anywhere in `e2e/` but that file. *Declined:* a reporter, which cannot see the browser; failing on hydration alone, since the measurement below found the suite's other console errors were a defect or a named refusal and nothing in between. **(2) Measured before turned on, and what it lets through is named.** A logging-only run found, besides the two defects (3), only Chromium's lines for refusals a journey provokes: `Failed to load resource` with a 4xx status (a signed-out probe's 401, a role's 403, an unknown address's 404, a taken address's 409); `net::ERR_INTERNET_DISCONNECTED`, from a request or AD-15's socket, under `context.setOffline(true)`; and the socket's upgrade refused with 401 after its session ended elsewhere. Those four patterns are let through and nothing else — a 5xx fails. The server's *destination stream closed early* (digest 2667547900, `apps/web/CLAUDE.md`) is a server log, not the browser's, and is out of the fixture's reach by construction. **(3) The sites were fixed first.** S-09 still failed to hydrate after 1abb3821, because `use-autosave.ts` treated `typeof navigator === 'undefined' || navigator.onLine` as offline, and Node has carried a global `navigator` with no `onLine` since v21, so the server drew the summary offline and the browser online; only an explicit `navigator.onLine === false` is offline now. The console's `SessionEnded` reads the refused address once rather than navigating from an effect keyed on the live `href`, which nested A-01's own address into each next `?redirect=` until React's update limit (#185); the journey (`e2e/admin/session.spec.ts`) asserts the `?redirect=` it lands with. |
| Report editing stays responsive — task 244 | **Set 16 Nov 2026, project owner** (*the pages related to report editing feel slow — slow scrolls and writing*; one phase, every recommendation of the analysis applied). Measured first on a production build at 4× CPU throttle, B1 with 85 controls: a keystroke inside a field took ~16 ms, but each commit blocked the main thread for about 200 ms twice and a keystroke waited 248 ms behind it, and a step change took 1.0–1.5 s with the old step looking idle. **(1) A commit re-renders the field it touched.** Autosave's state is published to a store (`client/selection/`) and a field selects its own entry — its acknowledged value, its save state, its findings — through `useSyncExternalStore`; `StepField` is `memo()`'d with one unit callback for the step; a reader that only writes reads `useAutosaveActions`, every step link among them. The context holding the whole state stays for the few screen-wide readers (the bar, the banners, re-authentication). *Declined:* a state library — the root file's four homes of state stand, and this is the reducer's own state, selected. **(2) A step change answers at once, and does not wait on a probe it does not need.** The navigation runs in a transition, and `StepBody` keeps the step on screen marked `aria-busy` and dimmed after 150 ms — S-07's *loading — refresh*, *prior content stays visible*. The task-92 probe is skipped while an answer within the last 60 s proved the session (a probe's `204`, an acknowledged flush); what that gives up is a session ended elsewhere within that minute meeting the sign-in screen with `?return=` rather than the dialogue, the unsent queue held in IndexedDB under the account as before. *Assumed:* the 60 s window, as the owner's recommendation left it unstated; widening or narrowing it is one constant. **(3) No activity statement while this process recorded the membership within the grain.** `MemberActivityStoreRepository` remembers each membership's activity as it last wrote it — only where its statement wrote — and sends nothing within the grain of that, since the column only moves forward; another replica, or a first request after a restart, asks as before. And `setTenantContext` binds both settings in one statement. **(4) The change counts stay counted by `entryCountsOf`.** Measured on the dev data: a whole report's history, 1,511 rows, read in 8.5 ms; a SQL `COUNT` would count rows where the footer counts statements that moved a registered field (task 84 row (2)), so the analysis's recommendation is *declined* on its own measurement. **(5) One statement per flush.** `DisclosureValueStore.writeMany` is `write`'s upsert over `unnest`, its guard per row — a computed or overridden figure declined and named, the rest stored — and a key named twice written once with its last contents; a lock or an archive still refuses the report from the trigger. **(6) One read per step.** `GET /reports/{id}/steps/{module}` (`StepPageController`, in `core/validation`, the module that already reads the wizard's and the comparatives' modules, so no cycle) answers the report, the module list, the step, last year's answers for the step's elements only, the last run and the rules, each as its own route answers it, the rules `null` where none can be read; the six routes stay for their other readers. Inside it `withSharedReads` lets the report and its stored answers be read once for every part — opt-in by this read-only route alone, so no request that writes ever answers from before its write. The NACE ancestry and the presentation precision are cached per registered version and per revision. |
| Monitoring a client's reporting, and the shared copy that makes its figures a tenant's own query — tasks 245 … 251 | **Set 17 Nov 2026, project owner**, promoting the monitoring half of the Corporate Buyer into MVP (`problem_overview.md` OQ-13; `use_cases.md` UC-216 … UC-235, D-17, D-18; `functional_requirements/12-monitoring.md`). The first customers are banks following their SME borrowers; the type is generic so a buyer following suppliers reuses it. **(1) A monitoring organization follows its clients both per client and in combined numbers across the portfolio.** It is a second typed relationship on FR-14's graph beside the advisor type, and its Administrator is the Organization Administrator of an organization of that type, as the Advisor Administrator is (182/2, 182/8). **(2) The numbers are live:** drafts included, not only filed reports; every figure shown to the monitor carries its state, *from a draft* or *from a filed report*, and totals say how many clients they cover and how much comes from drafts. **(3) The client's Organization Administrator grants a named monitoring organization read-only access to the whole report**, declines, or revokes at any time with immediate effect; the monitor can never edit, file or export on the client's behalf, and **there is no path by which a monitor attaches itself to an organization** (D-17). **(4) The monitor asks for a report** — year, scope (Basic or Comprehensive), due date — of one client or many, and progress is measured against the request: not started, in progress with a completion percentage, filed, overdue; it may change or withdraw a request. **(5) The monitor's Administrator manages its officers** (invite, remove, role) **and may limit each to assigned clients; by default an officer sees all clients**, and an officer's board and combined numbers cover only their assigned clients — mirroring 182/144's per-staff scope with the opposite default; the Administrator is bound by no limit. **(6) The combined numbers are built as a shared-figures copy owned by the monitoring organization.** While a grant is active and a report is named against a request, each numeric figure the client saves is also written, **within seconds, through the existing outbox and worker** (AD-6, AD-10), into a table that belongs to the monitor's tenant: client, request, taxonomy element, value and draft-or-filed state. The monitor's board, table and totals are **ordinary tenant-scoped queries over its own rows; no query ever spans tenants and the row-level predicate is unchanged** (AD-2, DR-5). **The copy is filled when access is granted and a report is named, and removed when access is revoked, the request withdrawn or the report un-named, so it is the consent boundary** (D-18). **A nightly job reports any disagreement between copy and source as an operational metric** — report, not repair — on the pattern of task 64's reconciliation of billing against the core. **The storage shape**: one tenant-scoped table in the core schema carrying the monitor's `organization_id` and the five columns above, with one progress row per named report beside its figures (assumption (c), OQ-63), with a client reference by id and the policy every core table has; its name and migration are task 249's. **Rejected: (A) iterating the roster with a scoped query per client, as UC-206 does** — right for a status board of at most twenty-five clients, too slow to sort, filter and total figures across hundreds, and each query would need the monitor inside each client's tenant in turn; **(C) widening the RLS policy to admit a grant holder** — it rewrites the predicate every core table depends on (AD-2, DR-5) and makes any mistake in the widened clause a cross-tenant leak, trading a copy that must be kept in step for a guarantee that is no longer unconditional. **Cost accepted:** a second copy of clients' numeric figures, a worker write on every save of a shared report, and a reconciliation to keep. **(7) Opening one client's report: the officer enters the client exactly as an advisor does** (FR-199, task 117's resolver) **but in a read-only role; the session resolves to exactly one tenant.** Access derives from two facts, membership of the monitor and the monitor's grant, and is stored nowhere else. **Each opening of a client's report by an officer is recorded and visible to the client's Administrator** (FR-220). **Calls made by the assistant and accepted by the owner.** **(8) What "whole report" covers: the client answers each request by naming one report**; the monitor sees that report and no other, so a 2026 request exposes no earlier year. **(9) A client may grant several monitoring organizations, each separately.** **(10) A grant lasts until revoked, with an optional end date** at which it expires automatically, defined as FR-195 beh. 3 and expired by the job of FR-203's shape. **(11) Adding a client:** the monitor gives the company's IDNO and a contact email; if the company is on the platform its Administrator receives the request, otherwise the email invites it to register and the request waits until the organization exists; nothing is shared until the client's Administrator grants. **(12) While a monitor has access, the client's report screen says that the named organization can see the report as it is filled in.** **(13) Every numeric figure in the standard is available** to the monitor's table; the defaults are Scope 1 emissions, Scope 2 emissions, energy, water, waste, headcount and accidents, **a recorded assumption** from conversations with prospective banks, to be revisited when a bank confirms (`functional_requirements.md` OQ-11, closed 17 Nov 2026). **(14) The monitor can download a client's exports once they exist, export its own board and figures to Excel, and send a reminder to late clients;** the existing deadline notices also serve a monitor's due date. **(15) Selling it — a monitoring plan and a client quota — waits with billing**; no use case or requirement is written for it. **Privacy-notice decision (17 Nov 2026, project owner):** a client's draft can be shared live with an organization the client approves, which is a new version of a legal document; the wording is drafted in the repository as provisional by task 246, as version 1.1 was for support requests, and monitoring access may be built and tested but is **not enabled for real clients until counsel has checked the text** (`design_spec.md` OQ-29). **Assumptions accepted, and what changes if each is wrong.** (a) The relationship states are the advisor's six (`pending`, `active`, `revoked`, `expired`, `declined`, `ended`), carried over whole; if the monitor needs a state the advisor does not, 245.1 adds it. (b) The table lives in the core schema because it is tenant-scoped and carries the row policy; if it belongs in a schema of its own, task 249 moves it before any data exists. (c) Only numeric figures are copied, beside one progress row per named report — its state, completion percentage and filed date (OQ-63, closed 17 Nov 2026); a narrative figure would be a different decision. (d) The Administrator sees every client, mirroring 182/144. **Open, recorded and not chosen:** how the one-named-report bound is enforced inside an entered session (OQ-62); the copy's lag (`non_functional_requirements.md` OQ-18); the points in `functional_requirements.md` OQ-10, OQ-12, OQ-13, OQ-15, OQ-16, OQ-17. |
| A locked tenant account released on A-02, with a reason — task 67.12 | **Set 18 Nov 2026, project owner**, who asked for every open question of task 67 to take the recommended option; 182/1 is the decision, and these settle the two points the task row left to its batch. **(1) The reason is a column of the system audit row.** `audit.system_audit_log.reason` — nullable, 1 … 500 characters and never blank by a `CHECK` — written by `AuditInterceptor` from the body field a route names with `@AuditAction({ …, reason: { fromBody } })`, trimmed, so the one row FR-209 behaviour 3 asks for carries the operator, the person, the action, the time and why, and A-08's log shows it under the action (`SystemAuditLogEntry.reason`). *Declined:* a JSON detail column, which would hold one field and invite others nobody declares; a second table keyed by the audit row, which a partitioned, append-only parent cannot reference by foreign key. A later action that asks for a reason declares the field and gains the column at no cost. **(2) A-02's member list says who is locked** — `locked`, from `identity.credential.locked_at`, which `esg_admin_ro` reads by a column grant on `(account_id, locked_at)` alone — so *Release* is offered only where it can succeed, and the 409 is a race, not the ordinary answer. **(3) The release is two statements on two roles**: membership read through `esg_admin_ro`, logged as an acquisition under the register's purpose, then `esg_app`'s `UPDATE identity.credential SET locked_at = NULL, failed_attempts = 0 … WHERE locked_at IS NOT NULL` — the reset link's own release — whose zero rows answer 409 `conflict`. Route: `POST /admin/organizations/{organizationId}/members/{accountId}/lockout-release`, audited as `admin.member_lockout.released`, the person's account its target. |
| Platform administration by roles of permissions — task 67.13 | **Set 18 Nov 2026, project owner**, each answer the recommended option (the owner's instruction for task 67); 182/3 is the decision and these are its batch. **(1) A permission is a closed vocabulary in code**, `ADMIN_PERMISSION`, one per guarded action or screen capability — seventeen, those of 67.5 … 67.8 declared now so the first catalogue covers them — and a route declares the one it needs with `@RequiresAdminPermission`, beside the class's `@RequiresAdminRole`. **(2) A role is a named set of permissions, and the set is code** (`CONSOLE_ROLE`, `CONSOLE_ROLE_PERMISSIONS`); **who holds a role is data**, `identity.admin_console_role`, one row per account and role, deleted when the role is taken away, its history the system audit log. The first catalogue is five roles drawn on FR-80's separations: *account administration* (accounts read and managed, roles assigned, the audit log), *support* (A-02's register and record, a phone, a lockout release, A-07), *operations* (A-18, A-17, A-21, taxonomy, migration runs, rules), *content author* (A-03 drafts and review) and *content publisher* (author's, plus publication). *Declined:* roles as configuration artefacts or as a table of their own, either of which lets an operator give a role a power with no reviewed change — what the separation exists to prevent. **(3) A Billing Operator holds no console role**: the realm stays that account's authority (NFR-65) until task 68 decides the billing screens' permissions. **(4) Nobody's power changed the day it shipped** (182/3's assumption, kept): the migration gave every Platform Administrator account not removed, and every pending Platform Administrator invitation, all five roles. **(5) An invitation names the roles its account starts with** — one or more for a Platform Administrator, none for a Billing Operator, refused 400 `validation-failed` otherwise — copied in the acceptance's transaction; the provisioning CLI gives its Platform Administrator all five, since the bootstrap's first operator must be able to assign. **(6) `PUT /admin/accounts/{accountId}/console-roles`** takes the whole set, at least one, under `accounts.roles.assign`, audited as `admin.account.console_roles_changed`; refused 409 `conflict` for one's own account (another administrator changes it, as with a suspension), a Billing Operator's or a removed one. Because the operator holds the assigning permission and cannot change their own roles, no change can leave the realm with nobody able to assign, so no last-holder count is kept. **(7) Roles are read per request, never sealed into the cookie**: `AdminRealmGuard` reads them for a route declaring a permission and refuses 403 `insufficient-role`, so a role taken away stops the account's next request; the session's answer carries `consoleRoles` and `permissions`, which the console's navigation and home read — presentation only, the guard being the boundary. **Why webhooks need their own bucket, and why 600.** Payment, MIA and e-Factura callbacks are
unauthenticated *by session* — they carry a provider signature, not a user token — so under the general
rule they consume the 60/min unauthenticated budget. That budget is per IP and every callback from one
acquirer shares one source range, which makes it a single allowance spanning every tenant's payments.
The consequence is specific rather than theoretical: §11.2 makes the callback the **only** authoritative
source of order state, so a throttled callback leaves a customer who has paid sitting in
`awaiting_payment`.

Steady-state volume at the stated envelope is single digits per minute and would never approach either
figure. The sizing case is not steady state — it is a backlog draining after a provider outage, which
DR-9 and NFR-54 already treat as expected behaviour rather than an anomaly. At ≤ 2,000 organizations on
monthly cycles the worst realistic backlog is roughly a day of callbacks; 600/min drains that in about
three and a half minutes, and leaves an order of magnitude over the renewal-day sustained rate. The
alert matters more than the ceiling: 70% sustained means the assumption behind the number has changed.

**An IP allowlist was considered and deliberately not adopted as the primary control.** It is the
stronger position — it would stop unknown traffic reaching a `@Public()` endpoint at all — but it
depends on the acquirers publishing stable ranges *and* announcing changes, which is not established
for maib, Victoriabank or MICB. A silently rotated range converts a delay into a hard 403 on every
callback, which is worse than the problem. It remains available as per-provider hardening wherever a
range is actually published; it is not what the correctness of the path rests on. Signature
verification in the adapter, and `(provider, provider_event_id)` de-duplication before any handler
runs, are.

Auth limits are tighter than the general API because NFR-64's uniform-response requirement means enumeration is bounded by rate, not by response difference. The export concurrency limit is a queue-depth guard, not an entitlement — entitlement quotas stay in the billing context under DR-1.

**The web session cookie and the CSRF stance — closing OQ-33 (21 Aug 2026, project owner, with
task 22).** `apps/web` holds AD-12's whole session in **one** httpOnly cookie: the access token,
the refresh token, both expiries and the session's identity block, sealed as a single AES-256-GCM
payload under `SESSION_SECRET` (node:crypto — no new dependency). Sealing is defence in depth on
top of httpOnly: the raw refresh token never leaves the Node tier in any readable form, and a
tampered cookie fails authentication of the ciphertext rather than reaching a parser. Attributes
as in the table above. `SameSite=Lax` rather than `Strict` because a top-level arrival from an
email link — a reset link, a notification deep link, UX-38's own re-entry path — must present the
cookie; under `Strict` every such arrival looks signed out and bounces to S-01. What `Lax` leaves
open (a cross-site top-level **GET** carries the cookie) is harmless by construction: GETs through
this tier are safe methods, and every state-changing request through `src/app/api/[...path]` must
additionally prove same-origin — `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin`, with an Origin/Host comparison as
the fallback where the header is absent, refused as a problem+json 403 otherwise. Server Actions
need no separate check: Next rejects an Origin/Host mismatch on every action POST (verified
against the pinned Next 16 docs). A per-session CSRF token (double-submit) was considered and
rejected: it adds plumbing to every client island and the autosave queue for a vector the
Lax-plus-origin-proof pair already closes, and it is revisitable without migration if a later
surface (an embedded widget, a cross-site POST target) changes the premise.

**Where the access token is rotated on a page load — task 26.4 (26 Aug 2026, project owner).**
The seal above holds a refresh token good for up to 7 days idle (the remembered pair; 12 h where the session was not — OQ-35 as amended), wrapped around an access token good for
≤15 minutes. `src/server/api/api-client.ts` attaches the sealed access token without rotating — it serves Server Components, where a cookie write throws during render — so with the gate checking only the cookie's presence, a member returning after twenty minutes to a screen that reads the API on page load (S-16 first) met a 401 while holding a session with six days left.

**`proxy.ts` is therefore the page-load rotation point**, alongside `src/app/api/[...path]` which
already rotates for client-island traffic. It is one of the two places Next permits a cookie write,
it already runs on every `(app)` request, and it runs *before* render — so the token the Server
Component reads from the cookie is the rotated one. `session.ts` single-flights refreshes per
token, which is what keeps a page issuing several parallel reads from spending the single-use
refresh token more than once; spending it twice past the race grace reads as theft and revokes the
session, which is the random-sign-out failure task 22 recorded and did not want to meet again.
Rotation is attempted only when the access token is within the refresh window and the request is
one that **reads** the session — the routes the gate admits, and since task 112 the two that issue
one, which resolve §4.3's branch during render and would otherwise do it with a stale token. A route
that does neither pays nothing, not even an unseal, and a failed refresh falls through to the
existing redirect rather than erroring, since an unrotatable session is one that has ended.

**The admin realm's session — task 23 (21 Aug 2026, project owner; sign-in is A-01's two-step handshake since the 24 Aug 2026 review, the drawn flow's *Signed in as …* a server-established fact).** OQ-17 put the token
handler on the api; these are the decisions that make it concrete.
The realm **mirrors the tenant session mechanism** — a ≤15-min JWT plus a rotating, single-use,
reuse-detected refresh token with task 21's race grace — rather than an opaque server-side
session, chosen for uniformity: one session model across both realms; the cost that bought — a revoked admin session's last access token honoured for up to 15 minutes, since the JWT is verified without a lookup until task 28's guard adds one — **closed with task 145 on 13 Sep 2026**, which reads the session on every admin request (§12.5.6's task-145 row). The pair never reaches the browser in
readable form: the api seals it, with the operator's identity block, into the httpOnly cookie
above and rotates it via `Set-Cookie` on its own responses. Separate tables
(`identity.admin_account`, `identity.admin_session`, `identity.admin_refresh_token`), separate
secret, separate cookie — NFR-65's "shares no session, cookie scope or credential" taken
literally. Sign-in throttles and locks exactly as §12.5.6's table says for every auth path; the
lockout's release is a PA action or the provisioning CLI, since the admin realm deliberately has
no password-reset flow. The lockout's release is A-08 (task 67.4, moved there 13 Sep 2026) or the provisioning CLI. **Set 12 Sep 2026, with the Stage 1 re-cut**, the realm gained its own credential surface: task 144 adds change-own-password, TOTP re-enrolment, recovery codes and a recovery sign-in that reaches a locked account, and task 151 gives the operator's own credentials screen A-19. The CLI stays the bootstrap (something has to create the first operator) and the last resort for an operator holding no unspent recovery code. With one operator, no recovery code and release behind shell access, the realm's recovery was a single point of failure no requirement had accepted.

#### 12.5.7 Retention for non-fiscal data

Completes what §18.2 recorded as partial. Required by the DSR runbook (NFR-28) and the exit runbook (NFR-31).

|---|---|---|

| Calculator inputs (`CALC_INPUT`) | **Permanent** | Already stated. Required by FR-45 … FR-47 comparatives and the audit trail |
| Generated exports (PDF, Excel) | Organization life + **1 year** | **Amended 5 Oct 2026** (project owner, task 182, 182/126), from 24 months: the export history stores the distributed file byte for byte (FR-53, `core.export_artifact`), regeneration cannot promise the original bytes (task 47.1), and a filed document is a regulatory record. Fiscal PDFs excluded; they follow the six-year rule |
| System audit, non-billing | **24 months** | |
| Disclosure audit trail (`core.field_change`) | Organization life + **1 year**; the trail lives and dies with its report | **Added 5 Oct 2026** (project owner, task 182, 182/126). NFR-29 keeps it for the life of the report. The bare actor id stays while the trail does, and a person's erasure does not overwrite it: that would be an exception to append-only (NFR-33) |
| Data-subject request record | **6 years**, the fiscal floor (BR-INV-7) | **Added 5 Oct 2026** (project owner, task 182, 182/127). One append-only row in `audit.system_audit_log` per request (FR-207), holding the ticket reference, kind, date and categories, and no personal data |
| Accounts never verified, or abandoned in setup | **7 days** from registration, then deleted with everything that cascades from the account by the worker's nightly sweep | OQ-52, and §12.5.6's task-200 row (**added 21 Nov 2026**). An address and a password hash whose only purpose has expired; until the sweep reaches one, the point-of-use rule already treats it as no account |
| Support requests (`identity.support_request`) | **24 months**, then deleted by the worker's nightly purge | **Added 30 Oct 2026** (project owner, task 77; §12.5.6's task-77 row (4)). A person's words and address, kept as long as non-billing system audit; the notice that delivered one to support is a platform notice's record, kept its own year |
| Metering events | **24 months** | NFR-47 cost attribution and FR-83's success metrics |
| Application logs | **90 days** | NFR-30 already forbids personal data in them |
| Error traces | **30 days** | |
| Billing audit, fiscal documents | **6 years** | Unchanged — NFR-72, DR-8 |
| Notifications, their deliveries and cancellations | Organization life + **1 year**; a platform notice — no organization — **1 year from sending** | NFR-109, and §12.5.6's task-50.1 row (19). Holds account ids, the addresses of recipients without an account, and a sealed link. **Enforced by task 163**: the worker's nightly purge, each table's `DELETE` policy carrying the period, an organization's end recorded when its row is deleted (§12.5.6's task-163 row) |

Erasure now has a defined behaviour for every category rather than only for fiscal documents via FR-130 — the gap `functional_requirements.md` OQ-5 and `non_functional_requirements.md` OQ-12 record. FR-207 is written against these values (5 Oct 2026), and closes the question in part.

#### 12.5.8 Redis durability, and backups

**Redis: RDB snapshots to a volume; AOF off; `maxmemory 2gb`; `maxmemory-policy noeviction`; alert at 70%.**

Three separate questions hide inside "does Redis need a volume", and they have different answers.

- **Is Redis a system of record? No**, and the volume does not make it one. PostgreSQL plus the transactional outbox remains the source of truth (DR-9, AD-6), and every outbox row carries an `idempotency_key`, so a replayed job is safe by construction.
- **Is a volume needed for correctness? No** — but only because of an invariant that must be stated rather than assumed: **an outbox row is not marked terminal until the work reaches a terminal state.** Without that, a job sitting in a delayed retry lives *only* in Redis, and NFR-107's exponential schedule is bounded at 24 hours, so a restart could silently drop up to a day of pending notification retries — and delivery records are compliance evidence under FR-170. The invariant is recorded here because it is load-bearing.
- **Is a volume worth having? Yes.** An RDB snapshot costs a few gigabytes and a brief fork at 2 GB `maxmemory`, and it turns a host reboot from "wait for the outbox relay to notice and re-enqueue everything" into a resume. AOF stays off: it buys per-write durability that nothing here needs, at a real write cost, and it is the option that would genuinely start making Redis look like a system of record.

**`noeviction` is the load-bearing setting, not the persistence choice.** The default `allkeys-lru` — and every other eviction policy — will, under memory pressure, silently delete a queued export or a pending e-Factura transmission with no error raised anywhere. `noeviction` makes the write fail loudly instead, so the worker retries and the alert fires. For a queue, evicting is data loss disguised as a cache miss.

**Backups** — pgBackRest to Scaleway `esg-backups`, continuous WAL archiving: weekly full (Sunday, outside the filing-window change freeze), daily differential, **35-day PITR window** (one filing-window cycle plus a month), 12 monthly fulls retained, 6 yearly fulls Object-Locked to match the fiscal archive. Restore rehearsal quarterly, satisfying NFR-36's **D** method.

**One rehearsal per year must restore to a host outside Hetzner**, from Scaleway using only the object store and pgBackRest. That is the rehearsal that actually exercises NFR-72's independence from the hosting provider, and it is what closes the substance of `non_functional_requirements.md` OQ-14 — a six-year statutory archive asserted to survive loss of the hosting provider, with, until then, no evidence that it does.

#### 12.5.10 The local development environment is the Compose stack

**Decided 18 August 2026. No service and no service client is installed on a developer machine.** PostgreSQL, Redis and the worker's document toolchain all run as Compose services locally, the same way they run in staging and production. A developer's host needs Node, pnpm, Docker and git — nothing else.

This is not only convenience. Three things follow from it that a host install would break:

- **Client and server versions cannot drift.** `docker compose exec postgres psql` is the client shipped inside the pinned PostgreSQL 18 image, talking to that same server. A Homebrew `psql` is a separate version on its own upgrade cycle, and the failure it produces is subtle rather than loud.
- **A host PostgreSQL can shadow the container.** A second server listening on 5432 means migrations apply, the application connects, and the two are different databases. This is the single most expensive local-environment failure available here, and not installing a server is the only reliable way to avoid it.
- **The document toolchain must be verified at the CI version, not the laptop version.** NFR-82's PDF/A-2a and PDF/UA-1 conformance is machine-validated by veraPDF, NFR-20's Excel check by headless LibreOffice, and both are gates. A Homebrew veraPDF on a Mac is a *different* validator from the one in the worker image; a local pass that CI rejects is worse than no local check, because it is trusted. **Each tool therefore lives in one image, exercised the same way locally and in CI** (amended 11 Oct 2026, project owner, tasks 44 and 46; §12.5.6's task-44 row (1) and task-46 row (h)): Chromium, qpdf and pikepdf in the `renderer` image §5 describes; veraPDF in a pinned image of its own, run by the export regression suite; LibreOffice in the test-stack image `infra/compose/calc`, which the Excel suites run and CI builds.

The consequence for §12.5.9's Chromium controls is that they hold everywhere by construction: there is one place the renderer is installed, so the assert-at-build check and the veraPDF re-validation on a Playwright bump cover local runs too.

**PostgreSQL is not PID 1 in the stack: the `postgres` service sets `init: true`** (15 Sep 2026). A process started inside the container whose parent dies there is reparented to the container's PID 1 — a healthcheck probe's child when Docker kills the probe at its timeout, and a `docker compose exec` can land there too. PostgreSQL 18's postmaster reaps such a process as an *untracked child process*, and for any exit status other than 0 or 1 it runs crash handling (`HandleChildCrash` in `postmaster.c` at `REL_18_4`): every connection is terminated and the server reinitialises. Under host load the stack's `CMD-SHELL` probe outlived its 5-second timeout, the orphaned `pg_isready` exited 2 (*no response*), and a browser suite lost its database for about 90 seconds. **Reproduced:** eleven crash recoveries in 100 seconds without `init`, none with it. `docker-init` reaps orphans and forwards the image's `SIGINT`, so stopping the service is still PostgreSQL's fast shutdown. **Declined, the exec form of the probe**: it avoided the orphan for `pg_isready` in the same test, but gives up the shell's expansion of `$POSTGRES_USER` and `$POSTGRES_DB`, and does nothing for an orphan left by `docker compose exec`. **Redis is unchanged**: its server has no crash path for a child it did not fork, and the same late-exiting probe left neither a zombie nor a log line. What would reopen this: an image whose entrypoint installs its own init, or a PostgreSQL release that stops treating an untracked child's exit as a crash.

**The suites run against a test stack of their own, never the developer's** (28 Sep 2026, project owner, task 174). `infra/compose/docker-compose.test.yml` is a second Compose project, `easyesg-test` — PostgreSQL on 5433 with database `esg_test`, Redis on 6380 — whose two services **extend** the dev file's, so the image pins, the healthchecks, `init: true`, Redis's `noeviction` and `init.sh` are declared once and only the ports, the database's name and storage differ. **Its data is in memory** (tmpfs): `pnpm test:down` discards it and the next `pnpm test:up` initialises a fresh cluster through `init.sh`, as CI's does. Every stack gate prepares it itself — `pnpm test:stack` brings it up, migrates it and seeds it from each one's pre-hook — and reads `apps/api/.env.test` — `DB_PORT`, `DB_NAME`, `REDIS_PORT`, the names every process already reads, committed because it holds no secret — as a layer over `apps/api/.env`: a single `node` command loads it as a second `--env-file`, which Node lets override the first, and a chain of commands, Playwright and Compose read it through `tools/with-test-stack.sh`; the browser suite's configuration refuses to start without those three, so a direct `playwright test` cannot reach the dev stack. **Why a stack and not a second database or a Redis index**: the suites shared the developer's store — overwriting an operator's provider configuration (task 172), failing provider journeys against a developer's enabled Google (task 173), and reverting migrations over the developer's rows; a second database beside `esg` would have left Redis shared, and a Redis logical database would have left pub/sub shared, since Redis channels span its databases. **`migrations:check` runs on both, and never destructively on the developer's**: apply, revert and re-apply with the invariants on the test stack; on the dev database only the pending migrations and the invariants, because a revert there rewrites whatever the newest migration's `down` drops — every credential's password-change date. **Task 172's snapshot-and-restore stays**, as suite hygiene rather than protection: each suite still leaves the test store as it found it, so no suite reads another's leftovers. **The browser suite keeps the dev application ports**, for `e2e/stack.ts`'s reason — the console inlines its api address at build, and a suite on ports of its own would test a different build. **What it costs**: a second pair of containers while tests run, and one `test:stack` per stack gate — about 2 minutes on a cold start that migrates from nothing, about 20 seconds warm, where it finds nothing pending and nothing to seed. **What would reopen this**: a suite that needs data the dev stack holds and the test stack cannot seed, or a need for the suites to run beside a developer's servers, which the shared application ports still prevent.

**Prometheus and Grafana run in the dev stack, behind a profile** (22 Nov 2026, project owner, task 202; §12.5.6's task-202 row). `pnpm dev:observe` starts the two beside the dev stack. Prometheus scrapes the worker a developer runs on the host at `host.docker.internal:9464`, and Grafana, on port 3400, opens on the raise-to-dispatch dashboard with no sign-in. They sit behind the `observability` profile so `pnpm dev:up` starts no more than it did on a memory-limited host. Their configuration is the one VM-3 is to load (task 257), so it lives in `infra/compose/prometheus` and `infra/compose/grafana` rather than in a development variant. The test stack runs neither: no suite reads a dashboard.

#### 12.5.9 Chromium pinning and upgrade verification

Chromium is **not separately pinnable** — it is derived from the Playwright pin. Playwright **1.62.1 ships Chromium 151.0.7922.34** (verified 18 Aug 2026). Three controls, which together are the upgrade-verification procedure OQ-27 records as missing (R-9, T-13):

1. Install explicitly — `pnpm exec playwright install --with-deps chromium` in the Dockerfile and in CI, at the pinned Playwright version. Never rely on `postinstall`, which pnpm 10+ blocks by default and which fails silently into a runtime PDF-export failure.
2. **Assert the resolved browser build at container build**, failing on mismatch, so a floating resolution cannot change the renderer unnoticed.
3. **Any Playwright bump re-runs the golden-report corpus through veraPDF** for PDF/A-2a and PDF/UA-1 before the bump is accepted. Tagged-PDF output is version-sensitive and NFR-82 is now machine-validated, so a renderer change is a conformance risk, not a patch bump.


## 13. Scalability, availability and performance approach

### 13.1 Performance targets

| Area | Target | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Interactive read | p95 ≤ 300 ms · p99 ≤ 800 ms at peak | NFR-37 |
| Autosave acknowledgement | p95 ≤ 250 ms, non-blocking, after durable commit | NFR-38, NFR-56 |
| Full-report validation | p95 ≤ 2 s | NFR-39 |
| Carbon calculation | p95 ≤ 1 s | NFR-40 |
| Entitlement decision | p95 ≤ 20 ms · ≤ 100 ms on cache miss | NFR-41 |
| Export | p95 ≤ 10 s; async + notification beyond 30 s | NFR-42 |
| Web vitals | LCP ≤ 2.5 s · INP ≤ 200 ms at p75, 4G mid-range | NFR-43 |
| Concurrency | 10× median with no maintenance window | NFR-44, NFR-48 |
| Notification dispatch | p95 ≤ 60 s from raise | NFR-106 |
| Content publish | ≤ 1 working day from approval, revertible in one step | NFR-85 |

### 13.2 How each target is reached

- **Interactive latency** is protected by moving all long-running work out of the request tier (AD-10) and by keeping the entitlement decision in-process (AD-5). NFR-46's verification is fault injection that floods the export queue while measuring NFR-37.
- **Autosave** batches debounced field-group `PATCH`es and runs only the validation rules touching the changed fields in-request; `RETURNING OLD/NEW` removes a lock and a round trip from that path.
- **Validation and calculation** are benchmarked against **maximum-population fixtures**, not typical ones.
- **Export throughput** scales by adding `worker` and `renderer` replicas; it is the binding constraint at the stated envelope.
- **Element-keyed reads** are served by indexes leading with `organization_id`, which every RLS-filtered scan predicates on.

### 13.3 Availability

| Aspect | Position |
|---|---|
| Targets | 99.5% outside the filing window, 99.9% inside it — **scoped to application availability, excluding single-host infrastructure loss** (§17.1) |
| Why the scoping is honest | `edge`, `redis` and VM-1 are each unreplicated. The three-VM topology buys durability, not uptime. Either the target excludes VM-1 infrastructure failure, or a second application VM is added behind the CDN |
| Maintenance windows | None announced inside the filing window (NFR-48) |
| RPO / RTO | ≤ 15 min / ≤ 4 h; **RPO = 0** for issued fiscal documents, payments and audit entries, delivered by scoped `synchronous_commit` (§10.2) |
| Degradation | Billing unavailable → the core keeps serving UC-17 … UC-48 on cached entitlements, open for granted keys, closed for new purchases (NFR-49) |
| Provider outages | Per-adapter outage simulation (NFR-50); an untransmitted invoice is a tracked exception, never a blocked checkout |
| Restore | Quarterly full restore rehearsal measured against both RPO and RTO (NFR-52) |
| Schema change | Expand → migrate → contract; nothing ships that cannot be reversed while the prior version runs (NFR-53) |
| Failover | A **manual runbook**. No automated promotion is specified — acceptable against RTO ≤ 4 h, but stated rather than implied |
| Reconnect | **A lost socket is not an outage** — every accelerated surface degrades to the poll that is its authority (AD-15), so a reader sees a correct screen on its own schedule rather than a broken one. That is the property that makes the manual failover above survivable at all: the reconnect storm behind a promotion is bounded by full-jitter exponential backoff to a five-minute cap, and clients that never reconnect keep working. No sticky routing, so a reconnect lands on any `api` replica |

### 13.4 Capacity and scaling headroom

At the stated envelope (≤ 2,000 organizations, ≈ 150 peak concurrent sessions, ≈ 200 export generations/hour, < 100 GB) this topology is comfortable, and the binding constraint is export throughput, which scales horizontally.

**NFR-45 requires accommodating 100× the envelope without redesign.** The migration path at that point is: managed PostgreSQL with read replicas, `worker` onto its own VM, and object storage already external. No part of this design has to be rebuilt to get there, which is the actual requirement.

Additional capacity mechanisms named in the sources: independent horizontal scaling of `api`, `worker` and `renderer`; a pre-window 10× load test and a 24-hour soak at 3×; a **partitioning plan gate for every append-only store** (NFR-8, NFR-46); and metering-derived per-organization cost attribution against the €0.50/free-tier-organization/month ceiling (NFR-47).
